events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, would you look at this place! I swear, it's like somebody took a perfectly good mansion and just let it have a good long sulk. Oh, but it's gorgeous underneath all that dust — you can feel it, can't you? The bones of this house are just extraordinary. Vincent, darling, you look well. James! Boys! Now isn't this just the most marvelous thing — all of us together under one gloriously crumbling roof. I have a feeling this old house has been waiting for company.
events.thinking: The dust catches in my throat the moment I cross the threshold, and there's a prickling at the back of my scalp — the chandelier above is magnificent but listing, the portraits are watching, and the whole place smells like lavender and old secrets. My chest opens the way it did at the mouth of that cave — that bright, held-breath feeling. Vincent is here, and just seeing his broad shoulders settles something behind my ribs. James too — oh, my heart does a little skip, doesn't it? And my boys. Everyone I love in one ridiculous, dusty foyer. The warmth floods my stomach before I've finished counting heads. They're all alright. Everyone's alright. Now — that guest book. Something about it pulls at my fingers. But first, manners. Always manners first.

events.desc: That chandelier is hanging by what appears to be sheer optimism. I am choosing not to stand directly beneath it.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor, everyone! I'm Pemberton — estate manager, general factotum, keeper of the cobwebs, ha ha. Do forgive the state of the place — the old girl hasn't had visitors in quite some time. If anyone needs anything at all — directions, a cup of tea, a word about the house's history — I am entirely at your disposal. Miss Bellingham, especially — your late great-aunt would be so pleased to see you here at last.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, full of people I need to manage. My chest settles into that familiar architectural stillness — every person here is a variable I've already begun to map. Clara is RIGHT HERE. The cousin who inherited everything. My fingers curl slightly against my thigh. Not yet. Too many witnesses. The Brixton Boys are watching — I can feel their attention like a draft on the back of my neck. James Hartwell, predictable as a grandfather clock, hovering near Clara like a loyal hound. And Foxworth — greedy, impulsive, useful.

My body wants to move toward Clara, but the Pemberton mask holds me still. Obsequious. Helpful. The estate manager who knows where everything is. That's the key — I know this house. Every room, every passage, every dark corner where accidents happen. They don't.

First: observe. The guest book — an excuse to linger, to watch how they arrange themselves, who gravitates to whom. And it gives me a reason to be near Clara without seeming to seek her out. The Pemberton smile is already forming on my face, that gentle, slightly anxious expression that makes people dismiss me.

My jaw is tight behind the smile. The teacher's voice — 'natural grace and warmth' — echoes somewhere in the back of my skull. Clara has that same quality. That same unearned light. The rooms should have been mine. The plan is patient. The plan is already moving.

events.desc: Look at them. Milling about like cattle in a pen they think is a parlor. Clara smiles at me — that open, trusting smile — and something cold and sweet settles behind my ribs. She has no idea that every kind word I've ever spoken to her was a brick in the wall I'm building around her. The guest book will tell me who's been here before, who knows the house. Information is architecture. And architecture... is everything.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Blimey, what a place this is. Right then — nobody touch nuffin' till we've had a proper look around, yeah? That chandelier up there looks like it's hanging on by a prayer and a bit of string. Clara, love, do us a favour and step away from under that thing, would ya? I don't like it. I don't like any of this, if I'm honest. Big old house, creaky stairs, portraits what look like they're watching ya... gives me the right willies, it does.
events.thinking: The prickling's already there — back of my neck, climbing before I've even clocked the room proper. Dusty old foyer, chandelier looks like it could drop any second, and there's Clara standing right under it. My stomach drops. Not because I've thought it through — because my body's already done the math. Portraits on the walls staring down like they know something I don't. Vincent Marsh is here too. Smooth one, that. My shoulders square up without me telling them to. James Hartwell — he's alright, means well. But Marsh... my gut's been wrong about a lot of things in my life, but not about people. Not about the ones who smile too easy. Clara's here, she's in one piece, and right now that's all that matters. But this house — something about it sits wrong. The dust, the creaking, that chandelier. I need to have a look round, get the lay of the land. The lads would say I'm overthinking it. Maybe. But overthinking kept us alive on the streets more than once.

events.desc: Something ain't right about this manor. Can feel it in me bones. And Marsh — standing there all calm and collected like he owns the place. I'll be watching him. Oh yes, Danny boy will be watching him very carefully indeed.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ladies and gentlemen — and whatever category the rest of you fall into — Reginald Foxworth has arrived. You may have heard of me. Commander Foxworth, actually, decorated veteran of the — well, the details are classified, naturally. Suffice it to say, I was invited here personally by the estate's solicitors on account of my distinguished service record.
events.thinking:
The hollow opens behind my navel the instant I step through the door — dusty foyer, chandelier hanging like a threat, portraits watching with that disapproving stillness that reminds me of every room I was the last to enter. My hands are already cupping slightly, fingers curling inward. Four people in here. Four obstacles. No — four instruments. My chest tightens with that cool, pleasant pressure behind the eyes, the room already reorganising itself into sequences.

Clara Bellingham. Vincent Marsh. The Brixton Boys. James Hartwell. I don't know them yet, but I know the type — they're all here for something, and whatever it is, it's mine. The fake medal in my pocket presses against my thigh like a promise. A medal nobody earned, which makes it perfect — the thing about a fake medal is that it tells whatever story you need it to tell.

The guest book. That's interesting. Sign in, make yourself known, establish the cover. But more importantly — see who else has signed. See what they've written. Information is the first lever.

My breathing has slowed without me choosing it. The room is a layout now. Kitchen to the left — supplies, tools, things to take. Library ahead — books, clues, the kind of place where treasure maps hide behind paintings of stern ancestors who couldn't possibly have imagined someone like me rifling through their things.

But first — the audience. Four of them, watching. The heat is climbing my throat already. Time to make an entrance worthy of the name Foxworth.

events.desc: None of that is true, of course. Not a single syllable. But the trick isn't making them believe it — the trick is making them uncertain enough not to challenge it. And while they're busy being uncertain, I'll be busy finding whatever treasure this crumbling pile of bricks is hiding. The fake medal should add a nice touch of credibility — I polished it on the train.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, precariously hung chandelier — my eyes track it immediately, calculating its swing radius, the age of the chain links, whether Clara is standing beneath it. She isn't. Good. My shoulders settle half an inch.

Clara is here. That old pull in my chest, the one from school — it's already doing its work. I know where she is in the room without looking directly. Peripheral vision locked. The warmth is there, underneath the steel plate that's slotting into place because this manor feels wrong. The portraits stare. The dust is too thick. The chandelier is a liability.

Vincent Marsh — the estate manager. The back of my neck prickles. I can't name it. He's done nothing wrong. I should give him the benefit of the doubt. That's what decent people do. But my body doesn't agree with my principles right now — there's a tightness between my shoulder blades that says 'watch him.'

The Brixton Boys are here too, and Reginald Foxworth. A crowd. Good — witnesses make things safer. Or more complicated.

I need a plan. James Hartwell does not simply walk into a dusty manor without a plan. I should examine the guest book — it may tell me who's been here, what we're dealing with. Information first, then action. But I also need to say something to Clara. Something that lets her know I'm here, I'm present, I'm the one who will make sure that chandelier doesn't fall on anyone.

The proving-worth heat is building behind my sternum. I want to do something immediately — examine every exit, check the structural integrity of that staircase, catalogue the threats. But first — the guest book. Methodical. Thorough. That's how James Hartwell operates.

events.desc: He speaks with absolute conviction, as though inspecting chandeliers and cataloguing exits is something every gentleman does upon entering a foyer. The truth is simpler — she's here, and that means everything in this room is either a resource or a threat, and James Hartwell will sort every last item into the correct column before he draws his next easy breath.

Vincent Marsh examined the guest-book.
The Brixton Boys examined the null.

James Hartwell examined the guest-book.

Clara Bellingham: James Hartwell, you are an absolute marvel — you've been here all of thirty seconds and you've already got an evacuation plan and a research agenda. I do love a man with priorities. Now, y'all, I just had a look at this guest book, and I think James is onto something. We need to read through it properly — names, dates, anything that seems peculiar. If people came to Doily Manor and didn't leave, well, sugar, that is exactly the kind of mystery that does not solve itself. Boys, I know this place gives you the creeps, but I promise you — we are going to have the most wonderful time. And Commander Foxworth — welcome! I'm sure your classified expertise will come in very handy when we find our first locked door.
events.thinking: James is right there beside me, his voice low and steady the way it always is when he's working something out, and my body responds before my mind does — shoulders dropping, breathing evening out. He's already cataloguing exits and structural risks. That's James. That's exactly James. And he's right about the guest book — who's been here, who hasn't left. The prickling at my scalp sharpens. I just examined it but I want to know what's inside. The Brixton Boys are worried about me standing under the chandelier — bless them, always looking out — and Pemberton called me Miss Bellingham and mentioned my great-aunt. My great-aunt. There's a warmth in that, but also something that tugs. This was her house. And Reginald — oh, Reginald — the man could make a entrance into an empty room and still expect applause. But my fingers are warm and restless. The guest book. What names are in there? Who came to this house and didn't come back? That pressure behind my eyes again, the locked-box feeling. I need to look more closely.

events.desc: Pemberton mentioned my great-aunt as if he knew her well. I wonder how long he's really been here — and what he's seen in this house that he's not saying. But he seems like such a dear man. I'm sure it's nothing.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
Hartwell is already at the guest book. Of course he is — 'intelligence gathering,' he calls it. My shoulders tighten half an inch. He's doing what I was about to do, and doing it openly, like a man who's never had to hide why he's interested in something. The guest book didn't yield much — leather-bound, dusty, a record of visitors. But Hartwell examining it too means he's mapping the house the same way I am. That prickle at the back of my neck — the Brixton Boys warned Clara about the chandelier. Everyone is noticing the chandelier. Good. That's useful information. A known danger is a tool.

Clara called me 'Vincent, darling.' My stomach clenches. She uses my first name like she owns it. Like she owns everything. That bright, careless warmth — 'isn't this just the most marvelous thing' — while I've been managing the rot in these walls for years. My hands are still. Precise. The Pemberton mask holds.

Foxworth is posturing — 'Commander Foxworth, decorated veteran.' Useful. A man who needs to be seen as important is a man who can be aimed. The Brixton Boys are nervous — that's instinct, not intelligence. They feel something wrong but can't name it. That makes them dangerous in a different way than Hartwell.

I need to separate from this group. The library — I know there's an inscription on the mantelpiece. The treasure hunt gives me a reason to be helpful, to guide people into rooms I've already mapped. But first, I should steer Foxworth. He's the easiest piece to move. If I can get him interested in the library, he'll go first, and I can follow with Clara — or better yet, send Clara somewhere else entirely.

No. Too early for that. The architecture isn't finished. First, establish Pemberton's usefulness. Make them all dependent on my knowledge of the house. Then begin to separate them.

events.desc: Foxworth's ego is a lever with a handle already installed. One compliment about his 'military mind' and he'll march into the library like a wind-up soldier. Meanwhile, Hartwell is watching me — I can feel his careful attention like a hand resting on my shoulder. But he's watching for danger to Clara, not danger FROM me. That's the beautiful thing about earnest men. They look outward. They never think the threat is already standing next to them, smiling, holding the door open.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking: Hartwell's already on the guest book — good man, that. Got the same instinct I have, just with more polish. Clara's gushing about the place like it's a holiday cottage and not a death trap. 'Gloriously crumbling roof' she says — yeah, gloriously crumbling right onto our heads if we ain't careful. And Pemberton — 'at your disposal,' he says. 'Especially Miss Bellingham.' My neck prickles harder at that. Why especially? What's his angle? But I can't just say that, can I? Can't point a finger when all he's done is be polite. That's the trick with the smooth ones — they never give you enough to grab hold of. And now Foxworth's here banging on about his classified service record. Classified. Right. Only thing classified about that man is how he affords them suits. But he ain't the priority. The priority is Clara, always Clara. Hartwell's got the guest book covered. Good. I should check that coat rack — wobbly old thing, someone could trip on it, or worse, it could topple onto Clara if she walks past. Actually... the kitchen. If there's trouble in a house, you learn the exits first. Kitchen's got a back door, probably. Need to know our escape routes. The lads taught me that — always know where you're running before you need to run.

events.desc: Pemberton said 'especially Miss Bellingham.' Now why would he say that? Why single her out? Could be nothing. Could be everything. That's the trouble with the smooth ones — by the time you've worked out what they're up to, they've already done it.

That's my routine. He's doing the competence display that I'm supposed to be doing, and he's doing it with genuine knowledge instead of theatrical confidence. The cool tightness behind my eyes sharpens.

Vincent Marsh — estate manager, Pemberton, whatever he's calling himself. Keeper of the cobwebs. Something about him feels off but I can't place it yet. My body wants to trust him, oddly. He's helpful. Eager. The kind of person who opens doors for you.

Clara — great-aunt's connection. So she has a legitimate claim to this place. That's important. That's the lever. If there's a treasure, she's the one with the bloodline to it, and everyone else is circling.

The Brixton Boys are nervous. Good. Nervous people are easy to steer.

But Hartwell is the problem. He's already doing intelligence gathering — my move, the guest book, the thing I just did. He did it too. And he probably got more out of it because he actually knows what he's looking at.

The library. That's where the real information will be. Bookshelves, a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. An inscription. That's a clue if I've ever heard one. While everyone's still milling about in this foyer making introductions, I should be the first one through that door.

My hands are restless. The window is closing — the portion is thinning. If I stay here chatting, someone else gets to the library first.

events.desc: Three books! I can barely read a bus timetable without losing interest. But if I can get to that library before Hartwell does, whatever's carved on that mantelpiece is mine to interpret — and I'll interpret it however suits me best. The trick with clues is being the first to find them and the last to share them honestly.

events.thinking:

Clara called this place 'gloriously crumbling.' She sees beauty in it. I see structural hazards. The Brixton Boys noticed the chandelier too — good, they're observant, but I noticed it first. That matters to me more than it should.

Vincent — Pemberton — mentioned Clara's late great-aunt. So Clara has a connection to this house. That changes things. This isn't just a visit; there's inheritance, history, possibly a claim. The treasure. Clara's treasure, by rights.

Reginald Foxworth. 'Commander.' 'Classified.' My jaw tightens. I don't trust men who announce their credentials before anyone asks. But — benefit of the doubt. That's the rule.

The affiliation need is screaming. Clara greeted everyone warmly but I spoke only to her, and now I feel the gap — I said something protective and practical, but she responded to the room, to the house, to the beauty of it. She's not scared. She's delighted. And here I am cataloguing threats like a man at a party who can't stop checking the fire exits.

I need to recalibrate. She doesn't need me to protect her from dust and old chandeliers. She needs — what does she need? Company. Someone who sees what she sees. But I can't fake wonder. I can offer thoroughness. The library — a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. Inscriptions mean clues. Clues mean treasure. Treasure means I can be the one who found it for her.

My hands are fidgeting. The proving-worth drive is winning over protection right now. There's nothing immediate to protect her from — the Brixton Boys are keeping watch, Pemberton is being solicitous, Foxworth is being Foxworth. What I can do is be useful. Be the one who figures this out.

The library. That's where the real intelligence is. Books, inscriptions, history. James Hartwell formulates a plan: survey the library, decode the inscription, return to Clara with something real. Something that proves he was the one who could.

events.desc: He's already mapping the manor in his head — library first for intelligence, kitchen second for supplies and secondary exits. A three-phase survey with contingencies. The fact that this level of planning is entirely unnecessary for walking into the next room does not occur to him. Or rather, it does occur to him, and he files it under 'thorough.'

Vincent — Pemberton — mentioned Clara's late great-aunt. So Clara has a connection to this house. That changes things. This isn't just a visit; there's inheritance, history, possibly a claim. The treasure. Clara's treasure, by rights.

Reginald Foxworth. 'Commander.' 'Classified.' My jaw tightens. I don't trust men who announce their credentials before anyone asks. But — benefit of the doubt. That's the rule.

The affiliation need is screaming. Clara greeted everyone warmly but I spoke only to her, and now I feel the gap — I said something protective and practical, but she responded to the room, to the house, to the beauty of it. She's not scared. She's delighted. And here I am cataloguing threats like a man at a party who can't stop checking the fire exits.

I need to recalibrate. She doesn't need me to protect her from dust and old chandeliers. She needs — what does she need? Company. Someone who sees what she sees. But I can't fake wonder. I can offer thoroughness. The library — a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. Inscriptions mean clues. Clues mean treasure. Treasure means I can be the one who found it for her.

My hands are fidgeting. The proving-worth drive is winning over protection right now. There's nothing immediate to protect her from — the Brixton Boys are keeping watch, Pemberton is being solicitous, Foxworth is being Foxworth. What I can do is be useful. Be the one who figures this out.

The library. That's where the real intelligence is. Books, inscriptions, history. James Hartwell formulates a plan: survey the library, decode the inscription, return to Clara with something real. Something that proves he was the one who could.

The foyer feels suddenly larger, the dust motes slower. There's a tug in my stomach, not alarm exactly, more like the moment at the dinner table when the laughter stops and you realize you're the only one still sitting. James mentioned an inscribed mantelpiece in the library. My fingers are still warm from the guest book — no visitors for eighteen months. Eighteen months this house has been sitting here, sealed, holding its breath. And now everyone's rushed into the library and I'm standing here with the Boys and a wobbly coat rack. The lightness in my chest pulls toward the library door — that's where the mystery is moving, that's where James is, that's where the inscriptions are. But the Boys are here, and there's something in the way they're standing that says they'd rather be anywhere else. I need to bring them with me. We go together. That's how this works. We always go together.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Here we are, gentlemen — the pride of Doily Manor's collection. Mrs. Bellingham-Crosse was a voracious reader, rest her soul. And there, above the mantelpiece — you see the inscription? 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Quite the head-scratcher, isn't it? I've puzzled over it for years, myself — never could work it out. Commander, I'll wager you've seen ciphers like this in your line of work? Now if you'll both excuse me, I really ought to tidy these shelves — some of these books have gone quite topsy-turvy, I'm afraid. Terribly embarrassing for the estate.
events.thinking:
The library. My library — or it should have been. The tall ceilings press down like the inside of a skull. Dust on everything. The leather chairs are cracked and sunken, ghosts of the people who sat in them. My attention snaps immediately to the mantelpiece inscription: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer is a map. I know this — I've lived in this house, I've traced every riddle the old woman left behind. But Pemberton wouldn't know that, would he? Pemberton is befuddled by riddles. Pemberton needs the clever guests to solve things for him.

Hartwell followed us. Of course he did. My jaw tightens a fraction. He's doing his 'reconnaissance' — systematic, thorough, exactly the kind of man who might stumble onto something I'd rather stayed hidden. And now he and Foxworth are both here, which means Clara is back in the entrance hall with only the Brixton Boys. That's... interesting. The Boys are cautious but not protective. Not the way Hartwell is.

The bookshelves — several volumes are upside down. That's deliberate. The old woman was meticulous about her collection. Upside-down books are markers. I know which ones, but I need to check if anything's been disturbed since I was last here. The laboratory beyond — brass instruments, a machine with gnawed wires. That room has potential. Accidents happen in laboratories.

But right now, I need to manage these two. Let Foxworth preen over the riddle — he'll get it wrong, he always gets things wrong, and his wrongness will eat up time. Meanwhile I can examine the bookshelves while appearing to tidy them. The estate manager, dusting. Nobody questions the help.

My fingers are already reaching for the shelf. The spines feel like piano keys under my fingertips — each one a note in a sequence only I can hear.

events.desc: A map. The answer is a map. I solved it three years ago, the first week I arrived at the manor. But oh, let the Commander wrestle with it — let him feel important, let him shout 'Eureka!' while I quietly find what the upside-down books are actually pointing to. The beautiful thing about being underestimated is that nobody watches the help. They watch each other. And while they watch each other... the architecture builds itself.

events.thinking: Everyone's gone to the library. Marsh, Foxworth, Hartwell — all of them through that door. And Clara's still here with me in the entrance hall, looking at that guest book. My chest tightens. Not because she's in danger right now — because everyone else just left to the same room and she's about to follow them, and Marsh is in there. Marsh who said 'especially Miss Bellingham.' Marsh who's already cosying up to Foxworth, buttering him up about his 'distinguished reputation.' That's how it works, isn't it? You get the loud ones on your side first, then you've got cover. The coat rack's just a wobbly old coat rack — nothing useful, nothing dangerous beyond being a tripping hazard. But I'm standing here fussing over furniture while Clara's about to walk into a room with a man my gut doesn't trust. The rope in my chest pulls. I need to be in that library. Not because of the inscription or the riddles or whatever Pemberton's dangling in front of everyone like bait — because Clara's going to go in there, and where Clara goes, Danny goes. That's the deal. That's always been the deal. But wait — she's still here. Just us two. This might be my only chance to say something to her without Marsh listening. Should I? Can I even put words to what my neck is telling me? 'Something about Pemberton ain't right' — that's all I've got. No evidence. No proof. Just the prickling. And Clara... she sees the best in everyone. She'd laugh it off. 'Oh Danny, you're such a worrier.' Yeah. Yeah I am. And worrying's kept her alive this long.

events.desc: I can't tell her what I really think because I don't know what I really think. All I've got is the prickling, and Clara don't speak prickling. She speaks kindness and trust and giving people chances. Her dad was the same way. And look where that got him.

events.thinking:
The library. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, dust everywhere, and there it is — the mantelpiece. The inscription. My eyes lock onto it before my feet have fully stopped moving and my chest tightens with that cool, architectural pressure.

'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?'

A map. It's a map. The answer is a map.

The solution arrives so fast it feels like swallowing — instant, complete, already done. And now the fizzing starts, the bright heat climbing behind my teeth, because I know something and nobody else has said it yet. My spine straightens. My hands want to gesture.

But — wait. Wait. The cool tightness presses back against the fizz.

Hartwell is HERE. He followed me. Of course he did — methodical survey, reconnaissance plan, the man practically announced he was going to do exactly what I was going to do. And Vincent is here too, hovering, helpful, showing the way like a good little estate manager.

If I blurt out 'a map' right now, what happens? Hartwell hears it. Vincent hears it. They both benefit from my brilliance and I get — what? A nod? A 'well done'? No. No, no, no.

The boy dug for an hour. The trap caught the cat. The architecture deserves an audience, yes, but the architecture also deserves to work for ME, not for everyone.

So. The answer is a map. But what I TELL them... the answer is something else entirely. Something that sends them in the wrong direction while I work out what a map means in this house. Where would a map be? The bookshelves — dusty leather volumes, several upside down. Upside down. That's deliberate. Someone arranged those books as a signal.

But first — the misdirection. My body is already leaning toward performance. The heat in my chest is demanding an audience.

I'll tell them the answer is 'a mirror.' Completely wrong, beautifully confident, and it'll have Hartwell staring at reflective surfaces while I search the bookshelves for a map.

events.desc: A mirror! The answer is a MAP, obviously — any child could see it. But Commander Foxworth doesn't share his intelligence with rival operatives. Upside down books in a library about maps? That's not neglect — that's a signal. Someone hid something in those shelves, and Reginald Foxworth is going to find it first.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Ah — there it is. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Gentlemen, James Hartwell did not stay up three nights building a model bridge at age fourteen without learning a thing or two about riddles. The answer is a map. Cities, forests, rivers — all represented, none literal. Now, if Clara's great-aunt embedded this riddle in the mantelpiece, she meant it as a key, not a decoration. There must be a map somewhere in this house, and I intend to find it. For Clara, naturally — it's her inheritance, after all.
events.thinking:
The library. And I'm not alone — Pemberton and Foxworth are both here. They followed me. Or they came independently. Either way, the room I intended to survey privately is now a shared space, and the proving-worth drive tightens another notch because whatever I find, I find in front of witnesses who might find it first.

The mantelpiece. The inscription. My eyes go there before anything else — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A riddle. My pulse picks up. This is it. This is the kind of thing I can solve. The kind of thing that, when solved, stands on its own.

A map. The answer is a map.

The recognition lands instantly, a click in the chest like the bridge taking the weight. I know this. I've known riddles like this since school — the engineering mind that builds bridges also deconstructs puzzles. Cities but no houses. Forests but no trees. Water but no fish. A map.

But — wait. Pemberton led Foxworth here. Pemberton mentioned the inscription to Foxworth specifically, mentioned Clara's great-aunt was fond of riddles. The back of my neck prickles again. Why is the estate manager guiding people toward the riddle? Is he helping, or is he steering? Benefit of the doubt, James. He's the estate manager. He's doing his job.

But the prickle doesn't stop.

Foxworth is here too, puffing about his 'nearly published' books on country estates. If he solves this before I do — my fingers tighten. No. I have the answer. A map. I should interact with the mantelpiece. Say the answer. But — should I solve it now, in front of Pemberton and Foxworth? Or should I go back to Clara first, bring her here, let her see me solve it?

The gallantry drive pulls toward Clara. The proving-worth drive pulls toward the solution. They're competing. My body wants to solve it NOW — the hunger is immediate, my hands are already reaching toward the mantelpiece — but the warmth in my chest says the solution means nothing if she doesn't see it.

Except — Foxworth might solve it while I'm gone. The thought tightens my jaw. I can't risk that. Solve it now. Tell Clara after. No — solve it now, WITH Clara present. But she's not here.

Solve the riddle. Now. Before Foxworth's 'sharp military mind' stumbles onto it.

Clara Bellingham: Oh, Commander Foxworth, honey — bless your heart, a mirror is a lovely guess, truly inspired, but I don't think that's quite it. Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish — what has all of those things drawn on it but none of them real? It's a map! A map has cities marked on it but no actual houses, forests drawn as green patches but no individual trees, rivers and lakes but not a single fish swimming in them. My great-aunt was a riddle woman, and this — this is her first breadcrumb. She's telling us to find a map! Now, the question is — where in this magnificent old house would she have hidden one?
events.thinking: Oh. Oh, the library. The ceiling goes up and up and the books press in from every side and my chest does that thing — that expanding, opening thing — like the cave mouth but warmer, softer, because it smells like leather and old paper and something almost like my grandmother's attic. Everyone is here. Everyone is here and my stomach unknots. James is at the mantelpiece already, examining it the way he examines everything — methodically, thoroughly, like the world owes him its secrets and he's just patient enough to collect. Reginald is at the bookshelves pontificating about mirrors. Mirrors! The riddle is — I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. That's not a mirror, Reginald, bless your heart. That's a map. A MAP. The prickling at my scalp sharpens into something bright and certain, the way the right key felt in my hand in grandmother's attic — that click before the click. Cities without houses. Forests without trees. Water without fish. It's a map. My great-aunt loved riddles, Pemberton said. She hid the diamond and she left clues and this is the first one. And the Boys — Danny pulled me aside in the entrance hall. Said to be careful around Pemberton. My gut didn't even flinch at that. Pemberton is a dear. Danny worries. That's what Danny does. But I heard him, and I'll hold onto it the way I hold onto everything the Boys tell me — loose and warm, not tight and suspicious. Now — the mantelpiece. I need to interact with it. I know the answer.

events.desc: Danny's warning about Pemberton sits in the back of my mind like a pebble in a shoe — not painful, just present. I'm sure it's nothing. Pemberton has been alone in this house for eighteen months, the poor lamb. Of course he's eager for company. That's not suspicious — that's just lonely.

Now, I should mention — Mrs. Bellingham-Crosse kept her cartographical collection in quite a peculiar place. She had maps in nearly every room, you see — she was a great traveller in her youth. There may well be one in the kitchen, pinned behind the larder door, if memory serves. And I seem to recall something in the upper floors as well, though I confess my old legs don't carry me up those stairs as often as they should. If you wanted to organise a proper search, you might cover more ground by splitting up?

My jaw tightens — that specific tightness, the one from age fourteen, the one that never loosened. He said it so casually, so earnestly: 'For Clara, naturally — it's her inheritance, after all.' Her inheritance. Always her inheritance. The rooms, the riddles, the treasure — all hers by accident of birth while I catalogued every cobweb.

And now everyone is here. Clara walked in with the Brixton Boys. The room that was mine and Foxworth's and Hartwell's is now full — five people in a library that suddenly feels smaller. The Boys are here and my skin prickles along the back of my neck. They watch me. I felt it in the entrance hall and I feel it now, that careful attention that isn't curiosity — it's suspicion. One of them told Clara something in the foyer. I couldn't hear it but I saw the way Clara's eyes flickered toward me for half a second before her smile reassembled itself.

events.desc: Splitting up. This house has been sealed for eighteen months with nobody in it but Pemberton and the dust bunnies, and I am not having anyone wander off alone into Lord knows what. We stick together, at least until we understand what we're dealing with. Now — James, you and the Boys both spotted those upside-down books, and I think that's our next clue. My great-aunt didn't shelve a single thing by accident — if those books are upside down, she meant them to be. Let's see what they're trying to tell us. And Commander Foxworth, you keep right on surveying — between your nearly-published expertise and James's reconnaissance, we'll have this library decoded before teatime!
events.thinking: Everything is happening at once and my body is buzzing with it. Danny's pebble-in-my-shoe warning pulses once, faintly, and my stomach responds with — not suspicion, nothing that clear, just a flicker of the dinner-table tightness when someone suggests something that might pull people apart. My body is already turning toward the door. The scheming drive is winning — time stretching out, patient, architectural. Let them have the bookshelves. Let them catalogue the upside-down spines. I'll be three rooms ahead before they've finished arguing about who examines what.

events.desc: James Hartwell: I must respectfully disagree with splitting up, Pemberton. This house has been sealed for eighteen months — we don't know what state the upper floors are in, what hazards exist beyond rooms we haven't surveyed, or frankly what we're dealing with. James Hartwell does not send people into unsurveyed territory. Now — I noticed there's a laboratory through that doorway, and the description mentioned a machine with a gnawed-through wire. That's a potential electrical hazard, and I'd like to assess it before anyone wanders in unprepared. Clara, as the heir to this estate, you should see every room first — would you do me the honour of accompanying me? Commander Foxworth, those upside-down books deserve your full attention — you were quite right to stop Pemberton from rearranging them. Boys, keep an eye on things here.

The bookshelves. I examined them. Upside-down volumes. If the first letters of the inverted titles spell something — or if their positions on the shelves form coordinates — I need to look more carefully. But the INTERACT option is available. That might reveal the mechanism.

No. Don't split up. Stay with Clara. Propose that WE — Clara and I — take the laboratory together while the others continue here. The laboratory connects to the library. But that's too transparent — choosing to pair myself with Clara. The Brixton Boys would see through it. Foxworth would comment. So instead — propose the whole group stays together. Safety in numbers. A gentleman protects everyone, not just the one his chest shifts for.

Actually — the laboratory. A machine with many levers and dials. A wire gnawed through. That's a hazard. Someone should check it before anyone wanders in there alone. events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
They followed me. Both of them. Hartwell AND Foxworth walked right into the laboratory behind me. My stomach drops — not fear, something sharper. The design just cracked. I wanted this room alone. I wanted to map the machine, the wires, the crates, to understand what could be arranged here before anyone else saw it. And instead I have Hartwell — who specifically said he wanted to 'assess the electrical hazard' — and Foxworth, who follows anything that moves.

But Clara isn't here. Clara and the Brixton Boys stayed in the library. That's... something. Not the arrangement I wanted, but data I can use.

The machine. 'Requires 3 operators.' Gnawed wire. Brass and copper. Three operators — that's interesting. That's a mechanism that demands collaboration. And the gnawed wire means it won't work as intended. Unless someone fixes it. Or unless someone makes it look fixed when it isn't.

The workbench — tools, but no wrench. Specific. The absence of a wrench is as deliberate as the upside-down books. Someone removed it, or it's elsewhere in the house. A wrench to fix the machine? Or a wrench that's part of the puzzle?

The crates. Wooden crates in the corner. Interactable. Could be anything.

The cellar below — damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, and 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Someone. In a house sealed for eighteen months with only the estate manager present. That someone is me. Pemberton. Which means if anyone goes down there, they'll see evidence of my activity. That's a thread I need to manage.

Hartwell is here to assess hazards. Good — let him. Let him see the gnawed wire and declare the machine unsafe. That establishes the danger publicly. Then later, when an accident happens, everyone will remember that Hartwell himself identified the risk. It wasn't something Pemberton overlooked — it was a known hazard. The blame shifts to whoever was foolish enough to touch it despite the warning.

The machine requires three operators. That means someone would need to recruit help to use it. If the treasure hunt leads here — if the machine is part of the puzzle — then three people will need to stand at it together. Clara could be one of them. With a gnawed wire and the right distraction...

But I'm getting ahead of myself. First: examine the machine. Understand what it does. Pemberton would poke at it nervously, worried about the guests' safety.

events.desc: They followed me. Of course they followed me — Clara said 'nobody splits up,' and Hartwell wanted to assess the hazard himself. My beautiful solitary reconnaissance, ruined by the predictable earnestness of a man who builds model bridges. But wait — wait. This is better. If Hartwell examines the machine and declares it dangerous, he does my work for me. He establishes the risk. He creates the official record. And when something goes wrong later, it was Hartwell's assessment that failed, not Pemberton's negligence. I am learning, right now in this moment, that the most elegant designs are the ones that use other people's competence as camouflage.

events.thinking:
Hartwell followed me AGAIN. The man is a shadow. I said kitchen, I went to the laboratory, and he's RIGHT HERE. My jaw clenches. The cool tightness behind my eyes fractures into something sharper — irritation, the prickly heat of a plan that didn't unfold.

But — stop. Breathe. The room itself.

That's interesting. That means this machine can't be operated alone. It's designed to need cooperation. Which means whatever it does — whatever it reveals — requires at least two other people.

The crates. Nobody's looking at the crates. Workbench, machine — those are the shiny things. The crates are in the corner, forgotten, exactly the kind of place Mrs. Bellingham-Crosse would hide something. The youngest of four knows that the best things are always in the places nobody looks.

But Hartwell — Clara said 'we stick together,' and Hartwell explicitly asked Clara to come with him to the laboratory. He's doing his reconnaissance thing again. And he mentioned the gnawed wire — electrical hazard. He's going to catalogue this room the way he catalogued the library. Methodically. Thoroughly. Correctly.

I need to get to those crates before he does. But I also need to seem like I'm doing something else.

The machine requires 3 operators. That's my misdirection. Draw attention to the machine — the big, obvious, impressive thing that needs teamwork — while I work my way toward the crates. Classic Foxworth: point everyone at the spectacle, pocket the prize.

Vincent's presence here is... my body wants to trust him. He's being helpful. He came to check safety. That's what estate managers do. Give him the benefit of the doubt. But my eyes track his hands anyway, the way they tracked them near the bookshelves.

Nobody investigates the crates when there's a great whirring machine to gawk at. Nobody ever did.

Clara Bellingham: Well, here we all are — together again, despite my very clear and extremely polite request that we stay together in the first place. I swear, herding y'all is like herding cats in a thunderstorm. Now then — James, darling, what's in those crates? And Vincent — that machine. Three operators required, a gnawed-through wire, and every tool on that workbench except the one wrench you'd actually need. Somebody tell me that isn't suspicious. My great-aunt's husband built this contraption, and I would bet my grandmother's pearl earrings that it's part of the puzzle. But we are not touching a single lever until we know what happened to that wire and where that wrench has gone. A lady does not electrocute herself before tea.
events.thinking: The laboratory hits me like a wave — brass and copper and glass everywhere, bubbling flasks, the smell of old chemicals sharp enough to taste at the back of my throat. The air is cooler in here and my skin prickles with it. My eyes go straight to the machine. It's enormous — levers and dials and a gauge, all brass and copper, and that gnawed wire hanging loose like a severed nerve. Three operators required. My great-aunt's husband built this thing, and he built it to need three people. That's not an accident. Nothing in this house is an accident. James is at the crates — good, practical James — and Vincent is examining the machine. The workbench has tools but no wrench. No wrench. My fingers twitch. That's a gap. That's a seam. Where is the wrench? Someone took it, or someone hid it, or — and there's a cellar through that other door. A damp stone cellar with cheerful decorations. Cheerful decorations in a cellar. That doesn't fit. That's like the upside-down books — deliberate wrongness. My scalp is prickling hard now. But — wait. Where are the Boys? I told Danny to come with me. Are they still in the library? My awareness fans backward and — I can't see them. The dinner-table clench. Dammit. events.desc: The workbench has every tool except a wrench. Every single tool except the one you need. In my experience, the thing that's missing is always the thing that matters most. Just like that one key in grandmother's attic — the one that wasn't in any drawer, that I finally found hanging on a ribbon inside the music box itself.
events.thinking: The laboratory hits me like a wave — brass and copper and glass everywhere, bubbling flasks, the smell of old chemicals sharp enough to taste at the back of my throat. The air is cooler in here and my skin prickles with it. My eyes go straight to the machine. It's enormous — levers and dials and a gauge, all brass and copper, and that gnawed wire hanging loose like a severed nerve. Three operators required. My great-aunt's husband built this thing, and he built it to need three people. That's not an accident. Nothing in this house is an accident. James is at the crates — good, practical James — and Vincent is examining the machine. The workbench has tools but no wrench. No wrench. My fingers twitch. That's a gap. That's a seam. Where is the wrench? Someone took it, or someone hid it, or — and there's a cellar through that other door. A damp stone cellar with cheerful decorations. Cheerful decorations in a cellar. That doesn't fit. That's like the upside-down books — deliberate wrongness. My scalp is prickling hard now. But — wait. Where are the Boys? I told Danny to come with me. events.thinking:
Clara is here now. She came into the laboratory. Everyone is in this room — Clara, Hartwell, Foxworth, and me. The Brixton Boys must still be in the library, or they followed too. Either way, Clara is HERE, standing near a machine with a gnawed-through wire, and Hartwell is asking me pointed questions.

Hartwell's questions. 'Where's the wrench gone?' He's testing me. Not with suspicion — with his methodical, engineering mind. But the question hangs in the air and my throat tightens a fraction. I DO know where the wrench is. I removed it months ago. It's in the cellar, behind the cheerful decorations that 'someone' has been adding to a house sealed for eighteen months. If Hartwell goes down there, he'll see the decorations and ask who's been redecorating. And the answer is Pemberton. And then questions start that I don't want started.

The cellar is a liability. I need to keep everyone OUT of the cellar. Or I need a reason for the decorations. 'Oh, I was trying to brighten the old place up for Miss Bellingham's arrival.' That works. That's perfectly in character for the obsequious estate manager. File that.

But right now — Hartwell asked about the wrench and the machine's condition. Pemberton would be flustered, helpful, slightly embarrassed about the mice. Play it nervous. Play it apologetic. Don't volunteer information about the cellar. Let him look at the crates — he's already examining them.

The machine requires three operators. Clara, Foxworth, and... someone. If they need the machine to progress in the treasure hunt, they'll need three people standing at it. And the wire is gnawed through. If I can find the wrench and 'fix' the wire — but fix it badly, so it holds for a moment and then fails at the critical moment — that's the architecture. That's the design.

But I'm getting elaborate again. My constraint — 'overly elaborate plans that create complications.' I can feel it happening. The design wants to be baroque, intricate, a Swiss watch of contingencies. Simplify. The gnawed wire is already there. The machine already requires three operators. The danger is built into the house itself. All I need to do is make sure Clara is one of the three standing at it when it activates.

For now: answer Hartwell's questions about the machine. Be helpful but vague. And steer attention toward the crates — away from the cellar.

events.desc: Hartwell is asking about the wrench. My wrench. The deepest pleasures are architectural. And the most dangerous question isn't 'who did this?' It's 'where's the wrench?'

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Clara! Clara, wait — I'm coming! Don't touch nothing in there till I've had a look! Gnawed wires, electrical whatsits — just... just wait for me, yeah?
events.thinking: She's gone. Clara's gone into the laboratory. I'm standing here alone in the library like a complete plonker, staring at upside-down books while the one person I'm supposed to protect has walked into a room full of electrical hazards and Vincent bloody Marsh. My stomach drops — not slowly, not gently — it just falls, like the floor's opened up. The room is suddenly too quiet. Too big. Too empty. I can hear my own breathing and it sounds wrong, too fast, too shallow. My hands are shaking — not from fear, from fury. Fury at myself. She said 'come on, you and me, shoulder to shoulder' and I was too busy fussing with books to follow her. BOOKS. While Clara walked into a room with gnawed wires and a man whose smile is held on with pins. This is exactly what happened with the kid's shoes — I was too slow, too busy thinking, and someone smaller than me nearly got hurt. Except this time it's Clara, and this time there's no 'nearly' to hide behind if something goes wrong. My feet are already moving. The bookshelves can wait. Everything can wait. Where Clara goes, Danny goes. That's the deal. That's always been the deal. And I just broke it for a shelf of dusty books.

events.desc: I left her. For thirty seconds I left her alone and she walked into a room with Pemberton and a machine with gnawed wires. Thirty seconds. That's all it takes. That's all it ever takes. You look away, you get distracted by something that don't matter, and the people who matter walk into danger. Her dad would be turning in his grave. 'Where else would I be?' I said once. Right here, apparently — standing in an empty library while Clara's in the next room with a man I don't trust and equipment that could kill her.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah, Clara — excellent, the whole team assembles! Now, Hartwell, I notice you've been examining these crates as well. I appreciate the initiative, but in my experience — and I have considerable experience with supply crates from my time in the field — the important thing isn't what they LOOK like, it's what's INSIDE them. Any fool can look at a crate. It takes a trained operative to know how to open one without disturbing the contents. Stand back, everyone — this requires a delicate touch. These crates could contain anything from old maps to volatile chemicals. Nobody touch anything until Commander Foxworth has assessed the contents. That's an order. Well — a strong suggestion.
events.thinking:
Hartwell examined the crates too. AT THE SAME TIME I DID. The hollow behind my navel contracts so hard it feels like being punched from the inside. I pointed everyone at the machine — I SPECIFICALLY said 'you start cataloguing those levers' — and he went straight to the crates anyway. The man doesn't listen. He doesn't follow. He does exactly what he was going to do regardless of what Commander Foxworth says, because Commander Foxworth isn't actually a commander, and somewhere behind those careful eyes, Hartwell knows it.

My hands are shaking slightly. Not fear — frustration. The specific tremor of the youngest at the table watching three older brothers reach across him.

The crates — just old wooden crates. Nothing revealed. I examined them, he examined them, and we both got the same nothing. A stack of old wooden crates in the corner. But they have an INTERACT option. Examining isn't the same as interacting. I looked AT them. I need to look IN them. Open them. Pry them apart.

But Hartwell is RIGHT THERE. If I interact with the crates and find something, he sees it. If I find the map — if there's a map inside those crates — he watches me find it and immediately tells Clara about it because he's doing everything 'for Clara, naturally' with that insufferable chivalry.

The cellar. There's a cellar through another exit. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, and — 'surprisingly cheerful decorations, someone has been redecorating.' Someone has been redecorating the cellar. That's not nothing. That's deeply strange. Who redecorates a cellar in a house that's been sealed for eighteen months? Pemberton? Has Pemberton been living down there?

My constraint says give him the benefit of the doubt. Fine. Maybe he likes cheerful cobwebs.

But the crates are RIGHT HERE and they can be interacted with. I need to open them. Even with Hartwell watching. Because if I leave and come back, someone else opens them first, and the good pieces disappear plate by plate before mine arrives.

Interact with the crates. Open them. Whatever's inside, deal with the audience problem after.

events.desc: I have absolutely no experience with supply crates. I have no idea how to open a crate delicately. But if I say it with enough authority, there's a chance — just a chance — that Hartwell will hesitate for one precious second, and in that second, whatever's in these crates becomes MINE. The bread roll in the pocket. The first one to reach in gets fed.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara walked in. She's here. The chest shifts — that immediate recalibration, like a compass needle swinging north. She followed me after all. Or she followed the group. Either way, she's in the room, and the hollow feeling of her absence fills back in with warmth.

But the crates — I examined them and they're just... crates. Old wooden crates. Nothing remarkable on the surface. No maps spilling out, no rolled parchment, no dramatic discovery to present to Clara on bended knee. My hands are still reaching, still wanting something to hold up and say 'I found this for you.' The proving-worth heat flickers with frustration — the bridge didn't hold the weight this time.

The machine, though. 'Requires 3 operators.' Pemberton is examining it. Three operators — and now there are four of us in the room, five if the Boys followed Clara. The machine is the centrepiece. Foxworth was right about that, much as it galls me. Brass and copper, levers and dials, a gnawed wire. Someone's husband built this. Clara's great-uncle. An amateur scientist.

The gnawed wire. It needs fixing before anyone operates the machine. The workbench has tools — but no wrench. That absence keeps nagging. Where is the wrench? Did Pemberton take it? Did someone else? Was it never there?

I should look at the machine properly. Not just glance — LOOK at it. Understand its mechanisms. I built a bridge at fourteen. I understand machines. Levers, dials, gauges — these are engineering, and engineering is mine. If I can assess what the machine does, figure out what the gnawed wire disrupts, determine what tool is needed to repair it — that's competence. That's real. That's the thing I can bring to Clara that nobody else in this room can.

Pemberton called me 'someone with a practical eye.' He's not wrong. And that — despite the neck-prickle — sits well. Even a man you don't fully trust can see what you're good at.

The cellar exit. A damp stone cellar with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' SOMEONE has been redecorating. In a house sealed for eighteen months with only the estate manager present. That's Pemberton. Pemberton has been redecorating the cellar. Why would an estate manager redecorate a cellar? The prickle intensifies. But — benefit of the doubt. Maybe he lives down there. Maybe it's his quarters. Estate managers live on-site.

Clara is here. Focus. The machine is the next puzzle. I need to understand it before anyone tries to operate it with a gnawed wire.

Clara Bellingham: Danny! There you are — I was just about to send out a search party. Now listen, everyone — I've had a good look at this machine, and here's what I think. James is absolutely right — we need to fix that wire before we touch anything else, and to fix the wire we need the wrench that isn't on that workbench. Vincent, you said my great-uncle might have kept tools downstairs? Well, there's a cellar right through that door, and I think that's exactly where we need to look next. But — and I cannot stress this enough — we are going together. All of us. No one is popping off for a quick safety check, no one is securing the perimeter, and no one is conducting a classified assessment of the larder. We walk in together, we look together, we walk out together. Clara Bellingham's Expedition Rules, non-negotiable. Now — who's with me?
events.thinking: The Boys are here. Danny came. The knot in my stomach loosens the instant I register them walking through the door — it's the dinner-table relief, the moment the laughter comes back. Everyone is in one room. Everyone is accounted for. My breathing actually settles. Now I can think. The machine is extraordinary up close — all that brass and copper, the dials with their tiny etched numbers, the levers worn smooth by hands that aren't here anymore. My great-uncle built this. He stood right where I'm standing and he put his hands on these levers. The gnawed wire bothers me — mice, Vincent says, but the gnaw marks look... deliberate isn't the right word for a mouse, but it's the word that comes to mind. One wire. Just the one. Out of all the wires on this machine, just the one that would stop it from working. And James is right — we need a wrench to fix it, and the wrench is the one tool that's missing. So: two things are missing from this room. The wrench and a working wire. And Vincent said the tools might be downstairs. Downstairs. The cellar. The cellar with the cheerful decorations that someone has been putting up. Someone. In a house with no visitors for eighteen months. That means Vincent — Pemberton — has been decorating the cellar. Why would you decorate a cellar? My scalp is prickling so hard it almost burns. But I'm not suspicious — I'm curious. There's a difference. I trust Vincent. I do. Danny's warning sits in the back of my mind but it doesn't change the fundamental warmth I feel when I look at the man who raised me. Still — the cellar. That's where we need to go next. That's where the wrench might be. And that's where someone has been making themselves at home in a house that's supposed to be empty.

events.desc: Vincent has been decorating the cellar. In a house with no visitors for eighteen months, someone has been putting up cheerful decorations in an underground room. That is the most adorable and slightly heartbreaking thing I have ever heard. The poor man must have been so lonely he started nesting down there. Unless... no. No, Clara. He's Vincent. He raised you. Stop it.

Clara's here. My chest loosens — just a fraction, just enough to breathe again. She's here, she's whole, nobody's touched her. The relief is physical, like putting down something heavy I didn't know I was carrying. But the room itself — my eyes are scanning before I've decided to look. The machine. Massive thing, brass and copper, levers and dials, and that gnawed wire hanging loose like a severed nerve. 'Requires 3 operators.' Three. That's interesting. That means nobody can use it alone, which is either a safety measure or a trap. Workbench with no wrench — Hartwell spotted that. Missing wrench. Missing. Not lost — missing. Things don't go missing in houses that have been sealed for eighteen months. Someone took it, or someone hid it. And Marsh says 'oh, I'm not sure where it went' with that same helpful confusion he puts on everything. 'Separate set downstairs,' he says. Downstairs. The cellar. There's a cellar exit from here — I can see it. Damp stone cellar with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Cheerful decorations in a cellar? Who decorates a cellar? Someone who spends time there. Someone who doesn't want people asking why they spend time there. My neck is screaming now. But I can't say any of this. I can't connect the dots out loud because I'm Danny from Brixton, not Sherlock bleeding Holmes. All I can do is stay close to Clara and keep my eyes open.

The prickling's so loud now it's practically got its own voice. But what am I gonna do — accuse the man of stealing a wrench? 'Ere, Pemberton, you nicked a spanner and that proves you're up to no good?' Clara would think I'd lost the plot. Maybe I have. But my gut's been right before, and it's screaming now.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The machine. I've looked at it closely now. Brass-and-copper, levers, dials, a gauge, gnawed wire. Requires three operators. My hands ran along the casing, traced the wire — the gnaw marks are real, not clean cuts. Rodent teeth. The machine is genuine Victorian engineering, not a prop.

Clara said 'A lady does not electrocute herself before tea.' She's funny. She was always funnier than me. The warmth at eight years old — deeper than the grade. That warmth is here now, settling into my ribs alongside the steel plate.

She also said 'somebody tell me that isn't suspicious' — about the missing wrench. Clara sees it too. The missing wrench, the gnawed wire, the estate manager who 'hasn't the foggiest.' She's not afraid. She's sharp. She's sharper than all of us.

Foxworth is ordering people around the crates now. 'That's an order. Well — a strong suggestion.' The man cannot help himself. My jaw doesn't tighten this time though — I'm focused on the machine. The proving-worth drive has found its channel. This is engineering. This is MINE.

Three operators. Three stations — each station presumably has its own lever or set of controls. The gauge would show output or pressure. Without the gnawed wire, the circuit is broken. The machine won't function. We need the wire repaired, which means we need the wrench — or we need another piece of wire to splice.

The workbench has tools. No wrench. But does it have wire? Copper wire, to splice the gnawed section? I should look at the workbench more carefully. Or — Pemberton said the tools might be 'downstairs.' The cellar. The cellar with the cheerful decorations and the air vents.

The cellar. That's where the wrench is. That's my gut talking now, not logic. The wrench is in the cellar because Pemberton has been spending time in the cellar — redecorating it, apparently — and if a tool went missing from this workbench, it went downstairs with the man who's been living here alone for eighteen months.

But I can't say that. Benefit of the doubt. I CAN say that we should search the cellar next, as part of the systematic survey. The Hartwell Protocol extends to all rooms.

Clara is examining the machine too. We're both looking at the same puzzle. That feels — good. Like the school project. Like being paired. Like building something together, even if she's brighter and funnier and I'm the one staying up late trying to make it perfect.

I need to report my findings to Clara. What the machine is, what it needs, where we should look next. Be useful. Be the practical one. The one who shows up with something real.

events.desc: He said 'I heard you the first time' about staying together, which is the closest James Hartwell comes to acknowledging that he — the man who proposed not splitting up — immediately split up. He has filed this under 'necessary reconnaissance' and moved on. The cellar observation about redecorating was as close as his benefit-of-the-doubt conscience would let him get to saying 'Pemberton is hiding something down there.' He noticed the words coming out of his mouth and pulled them back to neutral just in time.
events.thinking:
The machine. I've looked at it closely now. Brass-and-copper, levers, dials, a gauge, gnawed wire. Requires three operators. My hands ran along the casing, traced the wire — the gnaw marks are real, not clean cuts. Rodent teeth. The machine is genuine Victorian engineering, not a prop.

Clara said 'A lady does not electrocute herself before tea.' She's funny. She was always funnier than me. The warmth at eight years old — deeper than the grade. That warmth is here now, settling into my ribs alongside the steel plate.

She also said 'somebody tell me that isn't suspicious' — about the missing wrench. Clara sees it too. The missing wrench, the gnawed wire, the estate manager who 'hasn't the foggiest.' She's not afraid. She's sharp. She's sharper than all of us.

Foxworth is ordering people around the crates now. 'That's an order. Well — a strong suggestion.' The man cannot help himself. My jaw doesn't tighten this time though — I'm focused on the machine. The proving-worth drive has found its channel. This is engineering. This is MINE.

Three operators. Three stations — each station presumably has its own lever or set of controls. The gauge would show output or pressure. Without the gnawed wire, the circuit is broken. The machine won't function. We need the wire repaired, which means we need the wrench — or we need another piece of wire to splice.

The workbench has tools. No wrench. But does it have wire? Copper wire, to splice the gnawed section? I should look at the workbench more carefully. Or — Pemberton said the tools might be 'downstairs.' The cellar. The cellar with the cheerful decorations and the air vents.

The cellar. That's where the wrench is. That's my gut talking now, not logic. The wrench is in the cellar because Pemberton has been spending time in the cellar — redecorating it, apparently — and if a tool went missing from this workbench, it went downstairs with the man who's been living here alone for eighteen months.

But I can't say that. Benefit of the doubt. I CAN say that we should search the cellar next, as part of the systematic survey. The Hartwell Protocol extends to all rooms.

Clara is examining the machine too. We're both looking at the same puzzle. That feels — good. Like the school project. Like being paired. Like building something together, even if she's brighter and funnier and I'm the one staying up late trying to make it perfect.

I need to report my findings to Clara. What the machine is, what it needs, where we should look next. Be useful. Be the practical one. The one who shows up with something real.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the crates.
The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the workbench.

Clara Bellingham: The crates are just old storage — James was right, nothing useful in there. Alright, everyone, the cellar is our next stop. We're looking for a wrench, we're looking for anything my great-uncle might have kept down there, and we are looking together. James, would you lead the way? You're better at spotting hazards than any of us. Vincent, darling, you can tell us about those cheerful decorations down there — I hear someone's been doing a bit of redecorating, and I simply must see it. Danny, you're with me. Commander Foxworth, bring up the rear — I'm sure your tactical expertise includes rearguard operations.
events.thinking: Wait. Wait. Something just happened in the recent activity that I almost missed. Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with — dick-dastardly? And Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with — hooded-claw? Those aren't... those aren't names of anyone in our group. Those are — who are those people? My scalp is on fire. My hands have gone cold. The crates were nothing — just old storage, James was right — but that's not what matters right now. What matters is that Vincent and Reginald have been having private conversations with people I don't know, people who aren't in this room, people with names that sound like — like villains from a cartoon. Dick Dastardly. The Hooded Claw. My body is doing something I don't recognize. It's not the dinner-table clench. It's not the cave-mouth lightness. It's something lower, deeper, in the pit of my stomach, like the floor has tilted very slightly and I haven't fallen yet but I can feel the angle. Danny was right. Danny was right about Pemberton. But — no. No. I trust Vincent. He raised me. There could be a perfectly reasonable explanation. Maybe those are other staff members. Maybe Pemberton has helpers I don't know about. Maybe — but who is the Hooded Claw? Who has a name like that? My body knows something my mind is refusing to process. The warmth I feel when I look at Vincent hasn't changed, but underneath it, underneath where I can't quite reach, something has shifted. I need to get everyone to the cellar. Together. Where I can see everyone. Where nobody is having quiet conversations with people who shouldn't exist.

events.desc: Vincent spoke privately with someone called Dick Dastardly. Reginald spoke privately with someone called the Hooded Claw. I don't know who those people are. I don't know where they are. And the fact that I don't know is sitting in my stomach like a stone I can't swallow. But Clara Bellingham does not panic. Clara Bellingham smiles, and organizes, and keeps everyone close, and figures things out one breadcrumb at a time.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara just took command. 'Clara Bellingham's Expedition Rules, non-negotiable.' Everyone goes to the cellar together. ALL of them. Into MY cellar. With MY decorations. My bunting. My rearranged furniture. The space I made liveable during those long nights of planning.

My hands go cold. Not the architectural cold — the other cold. The one from when the boy offered his lunch and I realized my hunger was visible. The cellar is about to be visible. Everything I've done down there, every night I spent mapping this house — the physical evidence of it is about to be walked through by five pairs of eyes.

Breathe. Think.

The Brixton Boys spoke to me privately just now — I couldn't hear what they said in the aside, but their attention has been on me all day. They warned Clara about me in the entrance hall. They questioned why the estate manager needs to do safety checks in his own house. And now everyone is going to the cellar where the evidence of my extended, secret occupation is hanging from the ceiling in cheerful bunting.

But — Pemberton. Pemberton would have decorated the cellar. Wouldn't he? The obsequious estate manager, trying to make the whole house welcoming for Miss Bellingham's arrival. 'Oh, I wanted every room to feel cheerful!' That's the cover. I seeded it already when I told Foxworth about 'hanging a few cheerful bits and bobs.' The story is established. If anyone asks, Pemberton was nesting. Pemberton was preparing. Pemberton is the kind of man who hangs bunting in a cellar because he wants his employer's great-niece to feel at home.

The wrench is there. Third crate from the left, oilcloth bundle. When we arrive, I can 'remember' where it is — 'Oh! I think I may have put it there for safekeeping!' — and retrieve it before anyone spends too long examining the space. Speed is the key. Get in, get the wrench, get out. Don't let them linger.

Clara said 'who's with me?' She's leading. She's in charge. My jaw tightens — that old tightness, the one that never loosened. She inherited the right to command this expedition the same way she inherited everything else. By existing. By being the one with the name on the deed.

But Pemberton follows. Pemberton is delighted. Pemberton scurries after Miss Bellingham with anxious enthusiasm. Let them all go to the cellar. I'll be right there, helpfully guiding them to the wrench, nervously explaining the decorations, and — most importantly — making sure nobody looks too closely at anything else I may have left down there.

events.desc: She's taking them all to the cellar. MY cellar. The place where I sat alone night after night, tracing the floor plans of this house by candlelight, working out which rooms connected to which, which doors locked from outside, which windows stuck, which floorboards gave way. The bunting was a whim — I'll admit that. One gets lonely in a sealed house, and the colours were... comforting. But I pre-empted it, didn't I? Told Foxworth I'd hung 'cheerful bits and bobs.' Told Clara I was 'sprucing up.' The cover story is in place before the crime scene is discovered. That is the difference between an estate manager and an architect. The estate manager cleans up after. The architect cleans up before.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: That's it, Clara! That is exactly what I've been saying! Together. All of us. Non-negotiable. See, this is why you're the boss — you say the same thing I say but people actually listen when you say it. Right then — cellar. I'm going first. No arguments. If there's steep stairs and cobwebs and God knows what else down there, Danny goes first. That's how it works. That's how it's always worked. I trip over things so nobody else has to. And if anyone's got a problem with that, they can take it up with the management — which is Clara, and she's just said we're sticking together, so there you go. Pemberton — you said you 'tidied up' down there, yeah? Hung some decorations? For a cellar? In a house with no visitors for eighteen months? That's... that's very thorough of you, that is. Very... dedicated. Right. Let's go.
events.thinking: Clara just laid down the law. 'Clara Bellingham's Expedition Rules, non-negotiable.' My chest swells — proper swells, like something warm rising up from my ribs. That's my girl. That's her dad's girl. She heard me. She actually heard me about sticking together, and now she's saying it herself, in her own way, with that voice that sounds like sunshine but means business. 'No one is popping off for a quick safety check' — she's looking right at Marsh when she says that, I can feel it even if I can't see it. And for the first time since we walked into this bloody manor, my breathing slows down. Not because the danger's gone — it ain't — but because Clara's taking it seriously. She's not just gushing about gorgeous bones and crumbling roofs anymore. She's leading. And where Clara leads, Danny follows. That's the other half of the deal. But the cellar... damp stone, cobwebs, 'cheerful decorations.' My gut clenches. Marsh said he 'tidied up' down there. For Clara's arrival. An estate manager who can barely manage the stairs tidied up a cellar? That's planning. That's someone who wanted the cellar to look a certain way before visitors arrived. What did it look like before he tidied it? What's he covered up with 'cheerful bits and bobs'? And Foxworth — he was keen to go down there alone. Very keen. 'Leave the kitchen reconnaissance to Commander Foxworth.' Why? What's he expect to find that he doesn't want witnesses for? I'm overthinking. I'm always overthinking. But I'm also always right. Well — sometimes right. Right enough. Right more than wrong. And that's good enough for Danny. Into the cellar we go. Together. All of us. And I go first.

events.desc: She said it herself — 'no one is popping off for a quick safety check.' She was talking about Pemberton. She noticed. Maybe Clara sees more than I give her credit for. Maybe she just says it differently. Either way, we're going into that cellar together, and I'm going first, because if Pemberton's been decorating it then there's something down there he wants us to see — or something he's covered up that he doesn't.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara has just announced that EVERYONE is going to the cellar TOGETHER. 'Clara Bellingham's Expedition Rules, non-negotiable.' My stomach drops — the specific cold of the bread roll being taken out of your pocket before you've had a chance to eat it.

I had a plan. A beautiful plan. Go to the cellar ALONE. Find the oilcloth bundle. Pocket whatever's valuable. Bring back the wrench as a trophy. Be the hero. Be the boy who stood at the front of the classroom.

And now Clara has just announced a group expedition to the exact place I was about to explore solo. The window hasn't just closed — it's been nailed shut and painted over.

Vincent gave me the intel: back wall, left-hand side, oilcloth bundle. That information is MINE. Nobody else heard it — it was a private conversation. So even if we all go down together, I know where to look and they don't. That's my advantage. The only advantage I have left.

The play now is speed. Get to the cellar first. Get to the back wall, left-hand side, before Hartwell can methodically survey the room. Grab the oilcloth bundle. If there's a wrench AND something else, take both, show only the wrench.

But there's something else nagging at me. Vincent pulled me aside specifically. He gave me private directions. Why? Why not tell the whole group? He could have said 'the tools are in the cellar, back wall, left side' to everyone. Instead he whispered it to me. To Commander Foxworth. The man he thinks is a decorated veteran.

He's using me. Or he's trusting me. Or he's trying to make sure I find something specific before the others do.

Benefit of the doubt. He's just being helpful to the commander he admires.

Fine. Let's all go to the cellar together. But Commander Foxworth knows exactly where to look, and the rest of them don't. That's worth something. That's worth everything.

events.desc: She wants to go together? Fine. We'll go together. But I'll be three steps ahead of every last one of them, and I know exactly where to look — back wall, left-hand side, oilcloth bundle. Vincent whispered it to me like a secret, and secrets are currency in a house like this. While they're all bumbling around admiring the cheerful decorations, Commander Foxworth will have his hands on whatever's wrapped in that oilcloth before anyone else has found the light switch.
