events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara just took command of the entire group. 'Clara Bellingham's Expedition Rules, non-negotiable.' My chest swells — not with the proving-worth heat, something different. Something warmer. She did what I tried to do and failed at. She kept everyone together. She took my analysis — the wire, the wrench, the cellar — and turned it into a clear directive that nobody will ignore. Because when Clara says 'non-negotiable,' people listen. When James Hartwell says 'I propose a methodical survey,' people wander off to other rooms.

She's better at this than I am. The warmth at eight — deeper than the grade. She was always brighter, always funnier, always more capable. And I'm still the one staying up late trying to make it perfect while she makes people laugh and follow her with a single sentence.

But she said 'James is absolutely right.' She used my name. She credited my analysis. The wire, the wrench, the cellar — those were my observations, and she built her plan on them. The bridge held the weight. The judges wrote it down. She mouthed 'show-off' across the room.

The workbench. I examined it. Tools — screwdrivers, pliers, files, a small hammer, wire cutters. Wire cutters. And no wrench. The wire cutters are interesting — if we can't find the wrench, we might be able to strip the gnawed section and splice it using the tools that ARE here. Pliers to twist, wire cutters to trim. It's not elegant, but my father and the stranger fixed the car with what they had. You work with what's available.

But first — the cellar. Clara's calling everyone down there. 'Who's with me?' My body is already answering. Of course I'm with her. James Hartwell goes first into the unknown. That's the rule. That's the steel plate. That's the boy stepping between the older kids and the girl.

The cellar has cheerful decorations. Someone has been redecorating. Air vents line the upper walls. Air vents. Why would a cellar need air vents? Old houses have natural ventilation — stone breathes. Air vents are installed when you need controlled airflow. When you're doing something down there that requires it. Or when you're keeping something alive.

The protection drive surges. If there's something in that cellar — something Pemberton has been maintaining for eighteen months in a sealed house — then Clara walks in there over James Hartwell's body. Not before. Not without him in front.

'Who's with me?' she asked. James Hartwell is with her. Always. Since school. Since before he had words for it.

events.desc: Step zero of the Hartwell Protocol — the one he 'forgot to mention earlier' — did not exist until this precise moment. He has just invented a new prerequisite for his own three-step plan because Clara announced she was going first and every fibre of his being rebelled against the idea. The protocol now has four steps. By the time they reach the upper floors, it will have seven.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the cellar.
Vincent Marsh walked into the cellar.
The Brixton Boys walked into the cellar.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the cellar.
James Hartwell walked into the cellar.

Clara Bellingham: Oh, Vincent. Oh, you sweet man — you hung streamers. You actually hung paper streamers in the cellar. And paper flowers! Down here all by yourself for eighteen months, and you made it — you made it lovely. I could just about cry. Now, everyone — eyes open. We're looking for a wrench, or any tools my great-uncle might have stored down here. James, you mentioned he might have kept a separate set. This furniture has been rearranged very carefully — someone took real care with it — so let's check inside drawers, behind pieces, underneath anything that moves. And those air vents up there — I couldn't help but notice they're just about the right size for our mouse friends. The ones who supposedly gnawed through that wire. I have a feeling this cellar has more to tell us than it looks like at first glance.
events.thinking: The cellar. The cold hits my arms first — damp, the kind that gets into your bones and stays. The stone walls press closer than the rooms above, and my chest does that compressing thing, but it's not unpleasant — it's the cave feeling, the narrowing that means you're getting closer to something. And the decorations — oh. Oh, this is — streamers. Actual paper streamers, hung from the ceiling beams, some drooping with damp, some still bright. A few paper flowers. A small wreath on a nail. Someone — Vincent — has been down here making this dank stone box cheerful. My throat tightens. The part of me that tracks everyone's wellbeing, that notices when someone is upset or in trouble, that part aches. He's been alone. Eighteen months alone in a crumbling mansion, and he came down to the cellar and hung streamers. For whom? For himself? For us? The air vents along the upper walls catch my eye — small, a network of them, just big enough for something very small to explore. Mice? The mice that gnawed the wire? And the furniture — rearranged with surprising care, the description said. Not just stored. Arranged. Like someone was making a home down here. My curiosity pulls me toward the furniture — that's where tools might be hidden, where the wrench might be, where my great-aunt or great-uncle might have tucked away something important. But the air vents are nagging at me too. A network. Connecting to where? And everyone followed me down. Everyone. The group is intact. My stomach is as settled as it's been since we arrived. Now — find that wrench.

events.desc: One exit. One way in, one way out — back up through the laboratory. I have just led every person I love into an underground room with a single exit, and two of the people in this room have been whispering to strangers with very alarming names. Clara Bellingham, you are either the bravest woman in England or the most foolish. Possibly both.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Here we are — mind the last step, it's a bit uneven. Yes, I know, it's rather a state, isn't it? I did my best with the decorations — thought it might cheer the place up for your visit, Miss Bellingham. Your great-aunt always said a house should smile in every room, even the cellar! Now then — the wrench, the wrench... Mr. Bellingham-Crosse kept his good tools wrapped up to keep the damp off them. Let me just check the furniture — I have a feeling I may have tucked it away for safekeeping when I was tidying down here. Ah — yes! Here, I think — let me just...
events.thinking:
The cellar. MY cellar. The damp air hits my face and something contracts in my chest — not the architectural stillness, something rawer. This is the room where I was alone. Where I didn't have to be Pemberton. Where I sat in a chair I'd positioned facing the wall and traced floor plans by candlelight and the bunting overhead made the stone walls feel less like a tomb. And now there are five people standing in it, looking at everything, their eyes touching surfaces that were private.

The furniture — 'rearranged with surprising care.' My care. My arrangement. The chair facing the far wall where I could think without being watched. The side table where I kept the candle and the estate papers. They'll see how deliberately it was arranged. Not like storage — like habitation.

The air vents. I notice them for the first time from this angle — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Mice. The mice that gnawed the wire upstairs. The vents connect the cellar to the laboratory. That's... that's a detail I should have mapped before. A pathway. Something moves through those vents.

But right now — speed. Get the wrench. The furniture is interactable, and the wrench is hidden in it — behind or within the old furniture pieces. I need to go straight to it, retrieve it, and give everyone a reason to leave this room immediately.

The Brixton Boys' words echo: 'Very thorough of you. Very... dedicated.' The pause before 'dedicated' — I felt it like a finger pressing on a bruise. They're circling closer. Not close enough to name what they suspect, but close enough that the shape of their suspicion is starting to cast a shadow.

Act now. Before Hartwell starts his methodical survey of the room. Before the Boys start asking why the furniture is arranged like a living space. Before anyone notices the candle wax on the side table.

Pemberton would bustle. Pemberton would fuss. Pemberton would make a show of 'looking for the wrench' while going directly to where he knows it is.

events.desc: Move fast. Talk fast. Fill the room with Pemberton's nervous chatter so nobody has time to look closely at anything. The chair facing the wall. The worn spot on the armrest where my hand rested night after night. The candle wax pooled on the side table like a small, damning clock. Every surface in this room is a page from a diary I never meant anyone to read. Get the wrench and get them OUT.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah — the cellar. Exactly as I expected from Pemberton's briefing. Notice the air vents, everyone — standard Victorian ventilation system, connects to the rooms above. That's how the mice got to the machine upstairs — they're using the vents as highways. Fascinating from a tactical perspective. Now, the furniture — you'll notice it's been moved recently. But in my experience, when furniture gets moved in a sealed house, it's because something was behind it. Or inside it. I shall conduct a thorough examination — everyone else, fan out and check the perimeter. Those vents might tell us something about the mouse problem.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
The cellar. Cold hits my skin immediately — damp stone, the kind of cold that settles into your joints and doesn't leave. My muscles contract. The space compresses around me — low ceiling, stone walls, enclosed. My chest tightens, but not from the gallantry drive. This is the body registering confinement. One exit — back up to the laboratory. Only one way out.

The air vents. I look up and there they are — a network along the upper walls. My eyes trace them. They're not Victorian. The grilles are newer, cleaner than anything else in this house. Someone installed these. Recently. Within the last few years, at most. In a cellar. With only one exit.

Why does a cellar need ventilation?

The cheerful decorations — I can see them now. The furniture has been rearranged 'with surprising care.' This isn't storage. This is a living space. Someone has been DOWN HERE. Not visiting. Living. The furniture arrangement has purpose — comfort, not storage. The decorations are deliberate — someone wanted this space to feel inhabited.

Pemberton. Pemberton has been living in this cellar. Or keeping something — someone — here. The air vents, the decorations, the careful arrangement. My neck isn't just prickling now. My whole back is rigid.

Benefit of the doubt. Benefit of the DOUBT. Maybe he moved his quarters down here. Estate managers choose strange accommodations. Maybe the main bedrooms are too draughty, too haunted, too something. Maybe he decorated because he was lonely. Eighteen months alone in a sealed house — anyone would try to make their space cheerful.

But the air vents. You don't install air vents because you're lonely.

Clara is here. Everyone is here. The whole group, together, in a room with one exit. If something went wrong — if the door locked behind us — we'd all be trapped. My body has already mapped this: door behind us, stone walls around us, vents above us too small for anything except — the description said 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Mice. Rats. The thing that gnawed the wire upstairs.

The furniture. INTERACT is available. Something is hidden in or among the furniture. The wrench, maybe. Or the map. Or something Pemberton doesn't want us to find.

My hands are itching. The proving-worth drive and the protection drive are both pulling toward the furniture — one wants to find something useful, the other wants to find something dangerous before Clara does.

Clara asked me to lead the way. She said 'James, would you lead the way? You're better at spotting hazards than any of us.' My spine is straight. My breathing has deepened. This is what my body was built to do.

events.desc: There it is — the moment James Hartwell's two constraints collide head-on. His genuine belief in giving people the benefit of the doubt wrestling with his equally genuine instinct that something is deeply wrong in this cellar. He's asking the question as gently as a man can ask 'have you been keeping secrets in a basement?' — which is to say, not very gently at all, but with the sincere conviction that there must be a reasonable explanation. He wants there to be a reasonable explanation. His neck, however, has already decided there isn't one.

Vincent Marsh examined the old-furniture.
The Brixton Boys examined the old-furniture.
Reginald Foxworth examined the old-furniture.
James Hartwell examined the old-furniture.

Clara Bellingham: Vincent, darling — you tucked the wrench away for safekeeping? Well, that is just like you — always thinking ahead. Let's see it, then! If we can get that wire fixed, we can figure out what my great-uncle's marvelous machine actually does. James, you said the gnaw was between the second and third stations — do you think a simple splice will hold, or do we need to find copper wire too? And Commander Foxworth, that is an excellent observation about the vents — I hadn't thought of it that way, but you're absolutely right. If the mice came down through the ventilation to gnaw that wire, they must have a highway running through the whole house. Danny, sweetie, are you doing alright? You look a little peaked.
events.thinking: Vincent just said — 'let me just check the furniture — I have a feeling I may have tucked it away for safekeeping.' He tucked the wrench away. He tucked it away. The wrench that's missing from the workbench upstairs, the only tool needed to fix the machine — Vincent put it down here. My hands have gone still. Not cold exactly, but still, the way they go when something I was reaching for has changed shape in my fingers. He said he tucked it away 'for safekeeping.' That's — that's thoughtful. That's responsible estate management. That's exactly what a careful man would do with an important tool in a damp house with mice. It's perfectly reasonable. It is. But something behind my eyes has sharpened — that attic-key feeling, that pressure that won't release until the lock clicks. The wrench was removed from the one place it should be. The wire was gnawed through. And the man who removed the wrench is now reaching into the furniture to produce it, right on cue, as if this whole sequence was — no. No. Clara. He raised you. He's Vincent. He's being helpful. He's always been helpful. James is watching Vincent closely — I can feel it without looking. Danny spoke quietly to James just now. The Boys are worried. James is asking questions. And Reginald — Reginald mentioned mice using the vents as highways. That's actually brilliant, coming from Reginald. The vents connect the cellar to the rooms above. If mice gnawed the wire, they came through those vents. But — did mice really gnaw the wire? One wire? The exact wire? I need to look at those air vents. But first — watch Vincent. Watch what he pulls out of that furniture. And keep smiling.

events.desc: Vincent removed the wrench from the laboratory workbench. Vincent tucked it away in the cellar furniture. The only tool needed to repair the one wire that was gnawed through on a machine that requires three operators. I am watching the most attentive, most thoughtful, most suspicious sequence of coincidences unfold, and I am smiling through every single one of them, because Clara Bellingham trusts the people she loves, even when — especially when — the locked box in her grandmother's attic turned out to hold something other than what she expected.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Oh — oh, Miss Bellingham, you're too kind! I just wanted the old place to feel loved, that's all. Eighteen months is a long time to keep house alone, and your great-aunt always said the walls listen — so I thought I'd give them something cheerful to hear! Now, Mr. Hartwell — the air vents? Yes, those were Mr. Bellingham-Crosse's doing. He had them installed years ago — something about proper air circulation for his laboratory work upstairs. The vents connect through to the laboratory, which is why those wretched mice can move between the rooms so easily. I've tried blocking them, but... well, the mice always find a way, don't they? Ah! Wait — I think I remember now — the side table, there's a drawer — let me just check...
events.thinking:
Clara called me sweet. 'You sweet man — you hung streamers.' Something happened in my chest that I wasn't ready for. A loosening. A softening behind the ribs that has no architecture, no sequence, no plan behind it. For a half-second the room tilted and Clara wasn't the cousin who inherited everything — she was someone looking at my bunting, my paper flowers, the small desperate beauty I made in a stone room underground, and she saw it as kindness instead of loneliness. She almost cried.

And then the wall rebuilt itself. Faster than thought. The mineral weight dropped back into place behind my sternum and the loosening calcified into something I can use. She thinks I'm sweet. She thinks I decorated for HER. The cover story didn't just hold — it became something better. Something that generates trust. Something that makes her want to protect ME.

But Hartwell. He spoke to me privately — I couldn't hear everything but his tone was different. 'I'm asking as a friend, and I'm giving you the benefit of the doubt. But I am asking.' The air vents. He noticed they're modern. The Boys noticed the furniture arrangement. Two separate threads pulling at the same seam.

The furniture — I interacted with it but I didn't find the wrench. Hartwell is examining it too. Everyone is searching. I need to look more carefully — or acknowledge that the wrench might not be where I left it. Did I move it? Did I misremember? My hands are shaking slightly — not enough for anyone to see, but I feel it in the fingertips.

No. The wrench is here. It has to be here. I wrapped it in oilcloth and placed it... in the drawer of the side table. The one with the candle wax. That's where it is. The side table drawer.

Hartwell asked about the vents. I need an answer. The vents are — what? Mr. Bellingham-Crosse installed them. For his scientific work. For ventilation in the laboratory, which connects through to here. That's plausible. That's what Pemberton would say. 'Oh, Mr. Bellingham-Crosse had those put in — something about air circulation for his experiments upstairs. The vents connect the cellar to the laboratory, you see.'

But speed. Everyone is searching. I need to get to the side table, open the drawer, find the wrench. Before Hartwell does.

events.desc: She called me sweet. Nobody calls me sweet. The housekeeper called me 'such a helpful lad.' My guardian called me 'reliable.' The teacher called my cousin 'warm.' But 'sweet' — that word went somewhere I didn't expect, somewhere behind the wall, and for one terrible instant I felt the thing I cannot afford to feel: that it would be nice to deserve it. To actually BE the man who hangs streamers because he wants someone to feel welcome, instead of the man who hangs streamers because one day five people will walk into this cellar and need a reason not to ask questions. The architecture requires that I convert that moment into fuel. So I will. I always do. But my hands are still shaking.

events.thinking: Marsh is reaching into the furniture. 'Let me just...' — he's going for something. The wrench? Or something else? My body moves before my brain does — I'm stepping toward him, not away, because whatever he's about to pull out of that furniture I want to see it first. My hands are open but ready. Clara's behind me — good. Hartwell's watching too, I can feel his attention like a second pair of eyes. And Clara — 'Oh, you sweet man, you hung streamers.' My stomach drops. She's melting. She's actually melting over his paper flowers and his streamers and his 'your great-aunt always said a house should smile in every room.' And the worst part is — the absolute worst part — is that maybe she's right. Maybe he did just hang streamers because he's a lonely old man in an empty house who wanted to make it nice for Clara's visit. Maybe the decorations are exactly what they look like. Maybe the furniture was moved because he was tidying. Maybe the vents are just vents. And maybe I'm the paranoid idiot from Brixton who sees threats in paper flowers because a bloke in a suit took two kids off the street thirty years ago. But — but — Hartwell sees it too. Hartwell noticed the modern vents. Hartwell asked about the furniture arrangements. Hartwell 'gave him the benefit of the doubt but is asking.' So it ain't just me. Marsh is reaching into the furniture right now, saying 'I think I may have tucked it away for safekeeping.' The wrench that was missing from the workbench. He knows exactly where it is. A man who 'always gives this room a wide berth' and 'can't quite recall' where tools are kept — he knows exactly where the wrench is. Because he put it there. He moved it. Why would you move a wrench from a workbench to a cellar? Unless you didn't want someone to fix that machine.

events.desc: He walked right to it. Didn't search. Didn't rummage. Walked right to the exact piece of furniture and reached inside. A man who 'can't quite recall' and 'I'm not entirely sure' and 'if memory serves.' His memory serves fine when he wants it to. The question is why the wrench was down here and not on the workbench where it belongs. The answer my gut is giving me is: because someone didn't want that machine fixed. Not yet. Not until the right moment. Not until Clara was here.

Clara Bellingham: James — yes. Please. Go ahead and get the wrench. This is my great-uncle's house and his tools, and I'd like someone with steady hands and good sense to be the one handling them. Vincent, don't you fret — nobody's questioning your housekeeping, darling. You kept this whole place together for eighteen months all by yourself, and that takes a kind of devotion most people can't even imagine. Now — those air vents confirm what Commander Foxworth said about the mice having a highway through the walls. They connect right up to the laboratory. So we know how the wire got gnawed — if it was mice that did the gnawing. Once James has the wrench, I say we head straight back up, fix that wire, and find out what my great-uncle's magnificent contraption actually does. Three operators — that means three of us get to play. I'm calling first station!
events.thinking: James just did something beautiful. He asked for my permission. 'Clara, with your permission — your great-uncle's tools, your inheritance, your call.' My chest floods with something that's almost too big for the space — warmth and relief and a kind of fierce gratitude. He sees me. He sees that this is my house, my family's legacy, my decision. And he's not reaching into that drawer himself — he's asking me to decide who does. That's — that's James. That's the boy from school who always waited for you to go first through the door, not because he was afraid but because he knew it was yours to cross. The vents connect the cellar to the laboratory. That's confirmed. And they're new — James noticed that earlier, the grilles are modern. My great-uncle had them installed for his lab work. So: the vents are pathways. Things move through them. Mice, air, sound. What else? My fingers are tingling. The furniture has the wrench somewhere inside it — Vincent was reaching for a side table drawer. James wants to retrieve it himself. Danny is watching Vincent with that particular Danny intensity. Reginald is... being Reginald. Everyone is here. Everyone is watching. The cellar feels smaller with all of us in it but also safer — the cave-narrowing feeling, but with people I love pressed close on either side. I need to let James get the wrench. Then we go back upstairs, fix the wire, and see what this machine does. But I also need to talk to Danny privately. Soon. Not now — now we need to keep moving forward. But soon.

events.thinking:
Hartwell just took the wrench from me. Not physically — strategically. 'James Hartwell retrieves it himself.' He asked Clara's permission. Clara's permission. To handle a wrench that I hid in MY cellar. And Clara will say yes — of course she will — because Hartwell is the protector, the hazard-spotter, the man who builds model bridges and identifies structural weaknesses. The Boys called me out. 'Either your memory's a lot better than you let on, or you put it there yourself.' That landed like a slap — heat across my cheekbones, the sudden thinness of skin that comes when someone sees through a layer you thought was opaque. Danny notices things. Danny is the one I should have been watching all along, not Hartwell. Hartwell is predictable. Danny is instinctive.

My hands have stopped shaking. The wall is back. The mineral weight behind my sternum is solid again — the brief softening from Clara's 'sweet man' has been digested, metabolized, converted into something useful. She trusts me more now. She sees me as lonely and kind. That's a deeper foundation than mere helpfulness. That's emotional armor.

But the wrench. Hartwell is going to retrieve it. He's going to open the drawer, find it wrapped in oilcloth exactly as I described, and he's going to note that the wrench was moved deliberately from the workbench. He said so already — 'the wrench was moved deliberately from the workbench to the cellar.' He's not calling it sinister. Not yet. But the word 'deliberately' is hanging in the air like smoke.

Let him have the wrench. I can't fight this. If I insist on retrieving it myself, the Boys' suspicion sharpens. If I step back graciously, Pemberton is cooperative, transparent, nothing to hide. The obsequious estate manager who defers to the expert. That's the play.

And then — upstairs. The machine. Hartwell will repair the wire. Three operators will be needed. And somewhere in that sequence, between the repair and the operation, there will be a moment when the design can advance. Patience. The architecture is patient. The architecture is always patient.

events.desc: Let him have it. Let Hartwell open the drawer with his careful engineer's hands and unwrap the oilcloth and hold the wrench up to the light like he's found the Holy Grail. Clara Bellingham: Reginald Foxworth, you come back here this instant! I swear, that man has the listening skills of a — oh, never mind. He's gone. James, Danny — Reginald has just marched off alone to the library to chase a secondary cipher that I am ninety percent certain he invented on the spot. We need to follow him. Nobody should be alone in this house — I've said it three times now and I will keep saying it until somebody besides me and Danny actually listens. Vincent, darling, come along — we can search for the wrench when we've collected our wayward Commander. I will not have anyone wandering this house by themselves. Not on my watch.

Peter Perfect. The Ant Hill Mob. More names. More people I can't see, can't find, can't account for. First Vincent with Dick Dastardly. Then Reginald with the Hooded Claw. Now Danny with Peter Perfect and James with the Ant Hill Mob. Everyone. Every single person in this room has been having private conversations with invisible people with cartoon villain names. My hands have gone cold. Actually cold. The damp cellar air is pressing against my skin and I can feel every stone in the wall. This is — this is the cave. This is walking deeper when everyone else stopped. My heart is hammering the way it did when the walls narrowed and the light from the entrance became a pale grey suggestion behind me. But I kept walking then. I keep walking now. Because the crystal formation was real. The secret was real. And whatever is happening in this house — whoever these invisible people are — the answer is real too, and I will find it. But right now, right this second, Reginald has gone upstairs alone, and my body is pulling me toward the door to follow him, because nobody should be alone in this house. Nobody. Even pompous, self-aggrandizing Reginald Foxworth who can't follow a simple instruction to save his life. I need to pull Danny aside. I need to talk to someone I trust about what I'm seeing. But Danny is talking to Peter Perfect. Is there anyone in this house who is only talking to the people I can see?

events.desc: Everyone is talking to people who aren't there. Vincent. Reginald. Danny. James. Every single one of them. I am standing in a cellar surrounded by people I love, and every one of them has a secret conversation I wasn't invited to. The locked box in grandmother's attic held just old letters. But this locked box — this one — I'm not sure I want to know what's inside. I'm going to open it anyway.

Even pompous, self-aggrandizing Reginald Foxworth who can't follow a simple instruction to save his life. I need to pull Danny aside. I need to talk to someone I trust about what I'm seeing. But Danny is talking to Peter Perfect. Is there anyone in this house who is only talking to the people I can see?

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Hartwell and the Boys had a private conversation. I couldn't hear most of it, but I caught fragments in the keen observations — and what I caught freezes something deep in my gut. 'You watch Pemberton. I watch Clara. If Pemberton moves toward her when I'm at the machine, you step between.' They've formed an alliance. Against me. Not openly — Hartwell said 'I keep giving him the benefit of the doubt. Publicly. To his face.' They know. They don't have proof, but they KNOW. Danny said it: 'He's been setting the board. I just can't see what game he's playing.'

My skin is thin. Everything is thin. The cellar walls feel like they're pressing inward and my breathing is shallow but controlled — nobody can see it, nobody can see anything, because the Pemberton mask is the most practiced thing I own. But underneath, the architecture is cracking.

Danny noticed the dust on the decorations. 'The dust sits around 'em, not on 'em. They've been here longer than eighteen months of tidying up for Clara's visit.' That's the detail I missed. The dust pattern. The one variable I didn't control. I can control what I say, what I show, where I put the wrench, how I arrange the furniture. But I can't control how dust settles on paper flowers over time. The house itself is testifying against me.

And Foxworth just left. Walked out. Back to the library. The group is fracturing — but not the way I wanted. Foxworth is freelancing. Hartwell and Danny are a unit now. Clara is between them, protected. I am being hemmed in by people who smile at me while positioning themselves between me and my target.

Clara said 'if it was mice that did the gnawing.' IF. She's questioning it now too. The word 'if' — small, casual, devastating.

I need to redirect. The machine upstairs — Clara called first station. She WANTS to operate it. That's the opening. If I can't separate her from Hartwell and Danny physically, I need to make the machine itself the instrument. Hartwell will repair the wire. Clara will take first station. Two more operators needed. If Danny is watching me, Danny won't be at the machine. If Hartwell is watching Clara, Hartwell will be nearby but not necessarily AT a station.

Foxworth is in the library. Foxworth could be the third operator. Foxworth is easily managed.

But Hartwell said he'd check the gnaw marks — 'maybe someone who wanted a machine disabled would make a cut look like teeth marks.' If he examines the wire closely enough, he'll see what I did to it. The cuts weren't perfect. I was careful, but I wasn't a professional saboteur. I was a man with a pair of pliers and a plan.

I need to be upstairs when Hartwell examines that wire. I need to be there to distract, to redirect, to offer helpful commentary that steers his attention away from the cut edges. Pemberton, nervous about electrical things, hovering helpfully, asking too many questions — a nuisance that obscures rather than reveals.

Move. Now. Back to the laboratory. Before Hartwell gets there with the wrench.

events.desc: They've formed a pact. Hartwell and Danny, working together — one watches me, the other watches Clara. 'If Pemberton moves toward her, you step between.' The words I wasn't supposed to hear, cutting through the cellar air like wire through copper. And Danny — clever, instinctive, loyal Danny — noticed the dust on my paper flowers. Noticed that the decorations have been here longer than any visit could justify. The house is turning witness, and I am running out of rooms where the evidence doesn't speak. But there is one thing they haven't accounted for. They're watching ME. They're building walls between me and Clara. But the machine doesn't need me to touch her. The machine needs three operators. And Clara just volunteered to be one of them. All I need is to make sure the wire repair looks right but isn't. And for that... I need to be upstairs before Hartwell.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Hartwell got it. He got all of it. He said things I couldn't even think clearly — 'a wrench is a tool but it's also a weapon,' 'maybe someone who wanted a machine disabled would make a cut look like teeth marks,' 'a man who thinks he's unsuspected makes mistakes.' That's — that's everything. That's the whole picture I've been trying to see through frosted glass, and Hartwell just wiped it clean. And he said 'I'm promising you.' Not promising Clara, not promising her dad's memory. Promising me. Danny from Brixton. Like my word is worth making a promise to. My eyes are stinging and I don't know if it's the damp or something else. Doesn't matter. We've got a system now. I watch Pemberton. He watches Clara. Nobody gets between. And publicly, we keep giving him the benefit of the doubt. That's smart. That's smarter than anything Danny would've come up with. My plan would've been to corner Pemberton behind the bookshelves and shake him till he confessed. Hartwell's plan is better. Much better. Now — Foxworth just left. Walked right out. 'A secondary cipher in the stonework' — what a load of old cobblers. He's going back to the library alone, which is exactly what Clara said not to do. But that's Foxworth's problem. My problem is here: Clara, Marsh, Hartwell, the wrench. Clara's calling first station on the machine — of course she is, she throws herself at everything head-first, that's why she needs protecting. The machine that Pemberton might not want fixed. Or might want fixed at exactly the right moment. Hartwell said he'd check the gnaw marks. Good. Let him do that. I position myself between Clara and Marsh. That's my job. The wall. I'm the wall. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Hartwell and me. We've got a system. He watches Clara. I watch Pemberton. And Pemberton don't know we're watching. For the first time since we walked into this house, I feel like I can breathe. Not because the danger's gone — it ain't gone nowhere. But because I ain't carrying it alone anymore. Someone else sees what I see. Someone else promised. 'Where else would I be?' I said that once, outside a door, in the cold. Hartwell just said it back to me in different words. And he meant it too.

events.desc: Empty rooms. Empty corridors. Everyone in the cellar, two floors below, arguing over a wrench and a drawer. And Reginald Foxworth — Commander Foxworth — the man nobody takes seriously, the mirror answer, the nearly published author, the classified veteran of absolutely nothing — is walking through an empty laboratory toward an empty library with the one item in this entire house that fits the stone mantelpiece. They'll tell stories about this. The day everyone was digging in the cellar while the treasure walked out the front door in Commander Foxworth's pocket.
events.thinking:
I'm ALONE. For the first time since I arrived at this wretched house, I am completely, gloriously, beautifully alone. The laboratory stretches around me — brass instruments catching what little light filters in, flasks still bubbling softly on their stands, the great machine looming with its gnawed wire and its sign demanding three operators. But none of that matters right now.

What matters is what's through that doorway. The library. The mantelpiece. The inscription. And the fake medal in my pocket that the world has been telling me can be USED on that stone.

My breathing has changed. Slower. Deeper. The cool tightness behind my eyes has resolved into something pure — not the fractured irritation of competing with Hartwell, not the sour heat of botched misdirections, but the clean, settled architecture of a plan that has only one step left. Walk through that door. Put the medal on the mantelpiece. See what happens.

My hands aren't cupping anymore. They're still. Patient. The way they were when I watched the string pull taut on the cat trap, the counterweight shifting, the bucket beginning to tip. Everything in sequence. Everything inevitable.

Time is stretching. Not compressed like scarcity — stretched like design. They're in the cellar. Hartwell is opening a drawer. Clara is claiming first station on the machine. The Boys are watching the door. Vincent is hovering. None of them are thinking about the library. None of them are thinking about the mantelpiece. None of them remember the inscription that started all of this.

But I do. And I have the medal.

The library is one room away. Move. Now. Don't stop. Don't talk. Don't perform. For once in your life, Reginald, just — do the thing. Without an audience. Without the laugh. Without the speech.

The bread roll in the pocket. Nobody sees you take it.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Thank you, Pemberton — the side table with the candle marks. I see it. And for what it's worth — sitting by candlelight in a cellar because the house feels too big is not something a man should have to do alone. When this is over, we'll make sure Doily Manor has more company. Now — Clara, I'm retrieving the wrench. Danny, you're right here. Pemberton, thank you for preserving it in oilcloth — that's exactly what Mr. Bellingham-Crosse would have wanted. Once I have it, we go straight back up to the laboratory as a group — minus Foxworth, who has apparently decided that 'rearguard operations' means going back upstairs to look for imaginary ciphers. I'll deal with him when we get there. Clara — you called first station on the machine, and James Hartwell would not dream of disputing a lady's claim. But I am calling station two, and I am inspecting that wire before anyone touches a lever. The Hartwell Protocol, step two: repair before operation. Always.
events.thinking:
Foxworth just left. He walked out of the cellar back to the laboratory — alone. 'A secondary cipher embedded in the stonework.' The man who thinks the answer to a riddle about maps is a mirror now claims to see a secondary cipher nobody else noticed. His third book. Nearly published.

But — he's gone. And he's gone alone. Which means the group has fractured again despite Clara's rules. Foxworth is in the laboratory. We're in the cellar. Clara said nobody wanders off. Foxworth wandered off.

Does it matter? Foxworth can take care of himself. He's not the one I'm worried about.

What matters: Pemberton is here. Clara is here. Danny is here. I'm here. And Pemberton just pointed me to the side table with candle marks — 'I used to sit down here by candlelight when the upstairs rooms felt too big for one person.' God. That image. A man sitting alone in a cellar by candlelight because the house above him was too empty to bear. My callousness is 5/100. My chest aches for him. Even now. Even with Danny's words still hot in my ears.

The drawer. The oilcloth-wrapped wrench. Pemberton said it's there. Clara said 'please.' She said 'steady hands and good sense.' She's asking ME. My hands are steady. My sense is good. This is the moment — reach into the drawer, pull out the wrench, hold it up. The bridge holding the weight.

But I need to examine it. Danny said check it. A wrench is a tool but also — no. Pemberton isn't going to sabotage a wrench. That's paranoia, not caution. The man hung paper streamers because his employer said the walls listen. I can't — I won't — treat him like a villain without proof.

So: retrieve the wrench. Examine it briefly — weight, condition, any modifications. Then back upstairs. Fix the wire. Operate the machine. Find what Clara's great-uncle built it for.

Clara called first station. She's grinning. She's not afraid. She's excited. And that excitement — it does something to the warmth in my chest. It makes it lighter. Less like the country road, more like the engineering competition. Less fear. More possibility.

Get the wrench. Fix the machine. Impress Clara. Protect Clara. Same thing. Always the same thing.

events.desc: There — in the softness of 'a man should not have to do that alone' — is the real James Hartwell, the one underneath the protocols and the reconnaissance plans and the competitive jaw-tightening. He means it. He genuinely, completely means it. Pemberton may be hiding something. Pemberton may be setting the board. But Pemberton also sat alone in a cellar by candlelight for eighteen months, and James Hartwell's 5/100 callousness cannot walk past that without feeling the weight of it settle into his chest like his father's hand on his shoulder. The bravest and stupidest thing.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.
James Hartwell examined the old-furniture.
Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: The laboratory again. The brass instruments catch the dim light and throw it back in dull gold. Vincent followed me up — just Vincent. The others are still below. Danny and James are still in the cellar. I told everyone to follow and only Vincent came with me. My stomach is doing that thing again — not the dinner-table clench this time but something emptier, hollower, like the moment between when you call someone's name and they don't answer yet. Reginald is in the library. Danny and James are in the cellar. I am in the laboratory with Vincent Marsh. The man who raised me. The man Danny warned me about. The man who spoke quietly with Dick Dastardly. And I am alone with him. My hands aren't cold anymore — they're tingling, the way they do when I'm about to reach for something I know I shouldn't touch. The machine is right there. Three operators required. Gnawed wire. Missing wrench. And Vincent is standing beside me, helpful as always, charming as always, the warmth I feel when I look at him hasn't changed but there's something else now — something underneath the warmth, like finding a cold spot in bathwater. I can't name it. I don't want to name it. But my body is tracking him the way it tracks the space between arguing people at a dinner table. I should wait for James and Danny. I should not be alone with Vincent. But I am. And I need to decide what to do about that right now. I could pull him aside — ask him directly who he was talking to. I could. Clara Bellingham does not accuse. Clara Bellingham asks. But my suspiciousness is ten out of a hundred. My body doesn't do suspicion the way other people's bodies do suspicion. It does curiosity. It does care. It does the ache of wanting everyone to be alright. So I will wait here, by the machine, and I will talk to Vincent about my great-aunt, and I will wait for James and Danny to come through that door. And if they don't come soon, I will go get them myself.

events.desc: I am alone with Vincent Marsh in a room full of chemicals and a broken machine, and my people are scattered across three rooms despite everything I've done to keep them together. This is either the moment where I learn something true about the man who raised me, or it's the moment where I learn I should have listened to Danny from the start. Either way — I'm not afraid. Clara Bellingham walks deeper into the cave. She always has.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
I'm in the laboratory. Clara is here. Just Clara. Hartwell and the Boys are still in the cellar retrieving the wrench. Foxworth went to the library. For this one suspended moment, I am alone with Clara Bellingham in a room full of brass instruments and a broken machine.

My heart is hammering. Not in my chest — in my throat, in the thin skin behind my ears, in the pads of my fingers. Clara is RIGHT HERE. The machine with the gnawed wire is right there. The workbench with the pliers and wire cutters is right there. And the door to the cellar is behind me, with Hartwell and Danny on the other side of it, about to come through.

But I can't. Not now. Not like this. Pemberton doesn't attack. Pemberton doesn't grab. The scheme was never direct violence — it was architecture. Arrangement. Making the house do the work. And right now, if anything happened to Clara while I was the only person in the room, the case writes itself. Danny promised her father. Hartwell watches for hazards. If Clara gets hurt in a room where only Pemberton was present, every thread they've been pulling snaps into a noose around my neck.

So I stand here. In a room alone with the woman I came to kill, and I do nothing. Because the design isn't ready. Because the architecture isn't complete. Because doing it now, like this, would be simple and direct and CRUDE — the kind of thing a lesser man would do. Not me. Never me. I am not a man who pushes someone down stairs. I am a man who ensures the stairs are slippery at the precise moment the right person chooses to descend them.

Breathe. Pemberton. Be Pemberton. Clara is here. Say something helpful. Something warm. Something that makes her trust you more, not less. Because Hartwell and Danny are about to walk through that door with the wrench, and when they see you standing here with Clara, they need to see the estate manager fussing over the machine, not the wolf standing too close to the lamb.

The machine. I should be near the machine. Looking at it. Being helpful. Pemberton would be clearing clutter, wiping dust off dials, being useful. That's what they should see when they walk in.

events.desc: Alone with her. The room hums with the silence of almost. The pliers on the workbench catch the light. The wire hangs loose from the machine like a severed thread. And Clara stands there, bright and trusting, talking about her great-uncle's spirit as though spirit were something you could inherit along with the silverware and the deed. I could end this now. One push. One stumble into the machine. One 'terrible accident.' But the architecture forbids it — not because of conscience, no, never that — but because it would be inelegant. Because Hartwell would know. Because Danny would know. Because the plan I spent eighteen months building in a cellar by candlelight deserves better than a shove in an empty room. So I smile the Pemberton smile and I dust the dials and I wait for the wrench and the witnesses and the beautiful, inevitable moment when the design completes itself. Patience. The deepest rest lives on the other side of a finished design.

events.thinking: She's gone again. Clara walked into the laboratory. With Marsh. Without me. The tightening hits before the thought does — my whole chest seizing, my feet already turning toward the door. It happened again. I was standing here feeling good about my alliance with Hartwell, feeling warm about promises and systems, and Clara walked upstairs with the one person I'm supposed to be watching. The system. We agreed a system. I watch Pemberton. Hartwell watches Clara. But Hartwell's still down here getting the wrench from the side table, and Clara and Pemberton are both upstairs in the laboratory. Together. Without either of us. The warm feeling in my chest cracks like ice hitting hot water. How long? Seconds. Just seconds. But seconds is all it takes. The new kid cleaned out the stash in under a minute. The man in the clean suit had two kids in his car before anyone noticed. Seconds, Danny. Move. MOVE. Hartwell's got the wrench — he'll follow. My job right now is not to stand in a cellar feeling pleased about my new friendship. My job is to be upstairs, between Clara and Marsh, being the wall. Being the thing that has to be gone through. Foxworth's up there too somewhere — in the library chasing imaginary ciphers. So Clara's in the laboratory with Marsh and no one watching. No. No. Legs moving. Now.

events.desc: Every time. Every single time I stop moving, Clara moves instead. I stand still, she walks into danger. I talk to Hartwell, she goes upstairs with Marsh. I examine bookshelves, she wanders into a laboratory full of gnawed wires. The system only works if we're in the same room as the people we're watching. And right now, we're in the wrong room.

events.desc: This is it. This is the moment. The library, empty. The mantelpiece, waiting. The medal in my hand — fake, fraudulent, magnificent. Everyone is two rooms away arguing over a wrench while Commander Foxworth — Reginald Foxworth — the boy from the end of the table — places the only key that fits on the only lock that matters. If this works — if something opens, reveals, unlocks — then every humiliation today was just the string being drawn taut. The mirror answer. The splitting up that nobody agreed to. Clara's 'bring up the rear.' All of it was the boy digging the hole. And this — this right here — is the moment he looks up and sees who built it.
events.thinking:
The library. Silent. Empty. Dust motes hanging in whatever grey light creeps through the tall windows. The bookshelves with their upside-down volumes watching like a jury. The reading chairs thick with dust, nobody sitting in them, nobody watching.

And the mantelpiece.

It's right there. The carved stone. The inscription I can recite from memory now — cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. A map. Everyone knows it's a map. But the inscription is just the surface. The mechanism is underneath.

The medal is in my pocket. My right hand is already reaching for it. My fingers close around the cool, flat disc — fake gold, fake laurels, fake everything, the most honest object I own because it never pretended to be real to anyone except the people I showed it to.

My heart is hammering. Not the compressed panic of scarcity — something bigger, more open, the way it hammered when the string pulled taut on the cat trap and the counterweight began to shift. The moment before the bucket tips. The moment before you know if the architecture works.

The room is so quiet I can hear my own breathing. In, out. Slow. Controlled. The cool tightness behind my eyes has spread down through my shoulders, my arms, my wrists, all the way to my fingertips holding the medal. Everything is still. Everything is ready.

No audience. No Hartwell. No Clara with her 'bless your heart.' No Brixton Boys watching nervously. No Vincent hovering helpfully. Just me and the stone and the medal and whatever happens next.

The boy who hid the bread roll. Nobody saw him take it.

Use the medal on the mantelpiece. Now.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
Clara left. She went upstairs to chase Foxworth. Pemberton went with her. And I'm still in the cellar examining furniture that won't give me anything.

Clara is GONE. She's upstairs with Pemberton and Foxworth, and I'm down here with Danny, and the wrench is STILL in the drawer because I've been examining the same furniture three times instead of just opening the drawer and taking it.

My chest hollows. The country road feeling — the dark, the engine ticking, the smallness. She's up there and I'm down here. I failed at the one thing Danny and I agreed on: don't let Clara out of our sight. She walked out while I was giving a speech about candlelight and lonely estate managers.

The proving-worth drive was so busy performing — 'the Hartwell Protocol, step two' — that the protection drive lost her. Three times I examined the furniture. Three times. I could have opened the drawer, taken the wrench, and been at her side in the time it took me to narrate my own thoroughness.

Move. NOW. Get upstairs. Clara is with Pemberton and I am not there. Danny's right here — we go together. The wrench — I need the wrench. But I also need to be where Clara is. Both. I need both.

The drawer. The side table with candle marks. Open it. Take the wrench. Run upstairs. This is not the Hartwell Protocol. This is not a plan. This is a man realising he talked when he should have moved.

The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.
James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.
Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
They're here. Hartwell and the Boys just walked in. The brief moment alone with Clara is over — it lasted maybe thirty seconds, and in those thirty seconds she asked me what her great-aunt was really like. 'What was she like when it was just the two of you in the kitchen having a cup of tea?' And something happened that I can't name. A pulling sensation behind my ribs, downward and soft, like the ground shifting under me. Not the architectural stillness. Not the mineral wall. Something else. Something that wants to answer her honestly — not Pemberton honestly, but ACTUALLY honestly. Which is impossible. Because I never had tea with her great-aunt in the kitchen. I wasn't the estate manager here for the great-aunt. That's the cover. The real story is colder and has no kitchen in it.

But I didn't answer. Not yet. Because Hartwell and Danny walked in before I could speak, and the room changed. My shoulders squared without my permission — Danny's presence does that. Tightens the perimeter. My breathing went shallow and controlled, the Pemberton posture adjusting, weight shifting back from Clara, hands clasped in front of me. The helpful distance.

Hartwell has the wrench. I can see the oilcloth bundle. My oilcloth. My wrench. In his hands now. He's going to examine the wire. He's going to look at the gnaw marks with his engineer's eyes and his fourteen-year-old bridge-builder's memory and he's going to see what I did. Or he won't. The pliers left marks — small, clean, parallel. Mice teeth leave irregular, splintered marks. If he knows the difference — and he might, he might — then the architecture collapses.

I need to be talking when he looks at that wire. I need to be filling the room with Pemberton's nervous chatter, asking questions, being helpfully distracting. 'Oh, is that the wire? How dreadful! Do you think you can fix it? What tools do you need? Shall I hold the torch?' Pemberton the nuisance. Pemberton the bumbling assistant. The more I talk, the less he looks. The more questions I ask, the less space there is for the question he shouldn't ask.

Clara's question about her great-aunt is still hanging in the air. I need to answer it. A good answer — a warm, specific, Pemberton answer — will redirect Clara's attention to emotion, to family, to sentiment. Away from the wire. Away from the machine. Away from the dangerous mechanics of what's about to happen.

events.desc: I never met her great-aunt. The woman died before I arrived. Every word I just said was invented — a fiction built from the architecture of what Clara needs to hear, from the shape of the absence she carries, from the way her voice softened when she said 'one of the great sorrows of my life.' I gave her a kitchen, and a cup of tea, and a woman who missed her husband. I gave her an eleven o'clock ritual that never existed. I gave her the sentence 'houses don't forget the way people do' because I know — I KNOW — that Clara will hold that sentence in her chest like a coal and it will burn warm there for hours, and while it burns she will trust me more completely than she has trusted anyone in this house. And the terrible thing — the thing I will never say aloud, not even to myself in the dark — is that when I said it, something behind my ribs believed it too. For one half-second, I was the man who had tea with the old lady at eleven o'clock. And he was kind. And he was real. And then the architecture closed over him like water.

events.desc: It didn't work. The medal — my magnificent, polished, carefully-maintained fake medal — did absolutely nothing. 'Fussed with the mantelpiece,' it said. FUSSED. Like Commander Foxworth was rearranging the ornaments. I could weep. I could absolutely weep. But weeping is for people who give up, and Reginald Foxworth does NOT give up. He gives up on one scheme and immediately starts another, because that is what separates the truly committed fraud from the amateur. The medal was act one. The bookshelves are act two. Those upside-down books have been screaming their secret since we walked in, and while everyone else was too busy being useful to notice, Commander Foxworth noticed. He ALWAYS notices the thing nobody else is watching.
events.thinking:
'Fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.'

Fussed.

FUSSED.

The medal didn't work. It didn't click into place, didn't open a hidden panel, didn't reveal a map, didn't do ANYTHING. I pressed a fake medal against a stone mantelpiece and... fussed. Like an old woman adjusting doilies. Like a man straightening a picture frame nobody else will look at.

The hollow behind my navel doesn't open this time — it COLLAPSES. Caves in on itself like the hole behind the school when it rained and the mud slid back into place and there was nothing there, there was never anything there, and the boy who dug for an hour went home muddy and the boy who told the story went home empty.

My hands are shaking. The medal is — the medal is gone. My inventory is empty. It took the medal. The mantelpiece ATE my fake medal and gave me NOTHING. I fussed. That's the word it used. FUSSED.

The architecture didn't work. The string pulled taut and the counterweight didn't shift and the bucket didn't tip and the cat walked right past and nobody — NOBODY — was watching anyway.

I'm standing in an empty library with empty hands and an empty inventory, and in about thirty seconds everyone is going to come marching back up from the cellar with a wrench and they're going to find Commander Foxworth standing in front of a mantelpiece doing absolutely nothing.

Think. THINK. The medal is gone but the mantelpiece still says [USE, with: fake-medal] — no. No, it still shows [INTERACT]. Can I still interact with it? What does INTERACT do versus USE?

Or — the bookshelves. The upside-down books. Nobody ever interacted with those. Everyone examined them, looked at them, but nobody pulled the upside-down ones. The riddle answer was a map. The mantelpiece is a riddle. The books might spell something. The books might HIDE something.

I still have time. They're still in the cellar. The library is still empty. The medal was a dead end — a fake key from a fake commander — but the bookshelves are RIGHT THERE and they've been waiting since the beginning.

Don't stand here mourning a fake medal, Reginald. Move. The upside-down books. INTERACT with them. NOW.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara is here. She's HERE. In the laboratory. My chest releases — a breath I didn't know I was holding. She didn't go to the library after Foxworth. She came back to the laboratory. Or she was waiting here. Either way — she's in front of me, and Pemberton is here too, and Danny came up with me. Everyone is accounted for except Foxworth, who is presumably in the library chasing his imaginary cipher.

The relief is physical. My shoulders drop half an inch. The country-road feeling drains away and the steel plate softens. She's safe. She's here.

But I still don't have the wrench. I left it in the cellar. I examined the furniture three times and then ran upstairs without opening the drawer. The one thing I went down there to get — the thing Clara asked me to get, the thing Danny and I agreed was critical — and I don't have it.

My hands are empty. The hollowness behind my ribs — the kneeling-on-the-roadside feeling, watching someone else fix what I couldn't. I was supposed to retrieve the wrench. I was supposed to come back with something real. Instead I came back with nothing except panic and speed.

I need to go back down. Or — no. Don't leave Clara again. That's the whole point. Don't leave her.

But the wrench is downstairs. The machine is here. The machine needs the wrench. And I promised to fix the wire.

The cellar is one room away. Through that doorway, down the stairs, the side table with candle marks, the drawer, oilcloth-wrapped wrench. Thirty seconds there, thirty seconds back. But thirty seconds is how long it takes for everything to change. Danny said 'not for thirty seconds.'

Except — Danny is here. Clara is here. Pemberton is here. Everyone who matters is in this room. If I go down alone for thirty seconds, the only person at risk is me. And James Hartwell does not consider his own risk.

Go. Get the wrench. Come back. Fix the machine. Stop talking about it. Stop planning it. Stop narrating it. DO IT.

events.desc: For the first time since arriving at Doily Manor, James Hartwell has stopped planning and started moving. The Hartwell Protocol has been suspended. The bridge-building has been postponed. There is only a drawer, a wrench, and thirty seconds — and a man who has finally understood that the bravest thing is sometimes the simplest thing, done without an audience, without a speech, without a name.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the bookshelves.
James Hartwell walked into the cellar.
Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Danny doesn't know. He doesn't know who Peter Perfect is. He swore on my father's grave. And Danny — my Danny — would never swear on that grave unless he meant it with every fiber of his being. My father's grave is sacred to him. The most sacred thing. So either Danny is telling the truth and something is happening to all of us that we can't perceive — conversations we don't remember having with people we can't see — or... no. Danny is telling the truth. I know it the way I know the cave walls were real under my fingers. My body knows it. The warmth I feel when I look at him hasn't changed. It hasn't shifted. It hasn't developed a cold spot underneath. Danny is Danny. And he's scared. He said 'that scares me more than anything else in this house.' Danny doesn't say he's scared. Danny doesn't admit fear. If he's saying it out loud to me, it's real, it's deep, and he needs me to hear it. And he said something else — 'you watch me too. Watch everyone. Including me.' He's asking me to be the one who watches. Because he trusts me completely. The only person he trusts completely. And Vincent — Vincent just told me about my great-aunt. Tea at eleven. Two cups. She missed her husband. She left the riddles so the house would always have something to say. My throat is tight. My eyes are burning. The warmth I feel toward Vincent is different from the cold spot — it's real, it's genuine, and it exists alongside everything else. People are complicated. Love is complicated. And James has gone back to the cellar for the wrench. He'll be back. He said thirty seconds. Danny is here. We hold the line together.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob. I saw it. In the recent activity. I spoke to someone too. Someone I don't remember speaking to. Danny doesn't remember Peter Perfect. I don't remember the Ant Hill Mob. We are all talking to ghosts in this house, and not a single one of us knows it's happening. Whatever these invisible people are — whatever they want — they can reach all of us. Including me. Especially me. And I didn't even notice.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Miss Bellingham? Are you — are you quite alright? You look rather pale, if you don't mind my saying. And Danny — you too. Has something happened? I couldn't help but notice you both seem rather shaken. Is it the house? I know it can be unsettling — eighteen months alone here, I can tell you, I heard all manner of strange things. Creaks, whispers, shadows that moved when they shouldn't. An old house like this has a way of... playing tricks. If there's anything I can do — anything at all — please, you must tell me. Your safety is my first concern. Always has been.
events.thinking:
Something has changed. Something fundamental. Clara pulled Danny aside for a private conversation, and what I caught in the observations — it stops my blood.

Clara has SEEN my private conversations. She knows I've been talking to someone called Dick Dastardly. She knows Foxworth has been talking to someone called the Hooded Claw. She even saw Danny talking to someone called Peter Perfect, and Hartwell with the Ant Hill Mob. She's SEEN through the fourth wall. She's reading the architecture from the outside.

My throat is closing. Not visibly — the Pemberton mask holds — but inside, everything is contracting. The walls of the design aren't cracking anymore. They're dissolving. She knows about Dick Dastardly. She knows my TRUE identity is connected to someone — something — that exists outside the role of Pemberton. The name alone is a key that unlocks everything. If she researches it, if she connects Dastardly to the Hooded Claw to the Wacky Races — she'll see the pattern. She'll see what I am.

But wait. She also said Danny was talking to Peter Perfect. And Hartwell with the Ant Hill Mob. She's not singling me out. She's seeing ALL the private conversations, ALL the hidden identities. She doesn't understand what she's seeing yet — she thinks there are invisible people in the house. She's confused, not certain. And Danny is confused too — 'I don't know who Peter Perfect is.'

This is both catastrophic and... oddly equalising. If everyone has been seen with a hidden contact, then my exposure isn't unique. I'm not the only one with a secret conversation partner. But the NAMES. Dick Dastardly. The Hooded Claw. Those names carry a villainy that Peter Perfect and Penelope Pitstop do not. If Clara Googles those names...

Hartwell just went back down to the cellar for the wrench. He's not in the room. It's me, Clara, and Danny. Clara and Danny just had a conversation about invisible people in the house with villainous names. And they're both looking at me right now with a different quality of attention than they had five minutes ago.

The architecture is collapsing. The design that I spent eighteen months building in a cellar by candlelight — it's being unravelled not by evidence or deduction but by something I never planned for. Something impossible. Clara can SEE what shouldn't be visible.

Self-preservation. Now. Right now. The Pemberton mask must hold harder than it has ever held. Be confused. Be concerned. Be the helpful estate manager who is ALSO worried about invisible people in the house. If everyone is suspicious, then Pemberton should be suspicious too. Match their energy. Join their fear. Become an ally in the mystery rather than its subject.

events.desc: She knows. She doesn't know WHAT she knows, but she knows. Dick Dastardly. The name of the man behind the man behind the mask. Spoken aloud in a cellar by a woman who shouldn't be able to see him. The architecture — my beautiful, patient, eighteen-month architecture — is being dismantled by something I cannot map, cannot predict, cannot control. And for the first time since I was fifteen years old, sitting in a dead man's study with the keys to a house that should have been mine, I feel the thing I taught myself never to feel again: the ground moving under me without my permission. The design is not finished. The design may never be finished. And the deepest rest I've ever known — the dreamless sleep on the other side of a completed plan — is receding like a tide I can't call back.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Hartwell's gone back to the cellar for the wrench. It's just me, Clara, and Marsh in the laboratory now. My eyes snap to Marsh — what's he doing? Standing there. Talking about Clara's great-aunt. Making tea at eleven o'clock. Two cups. 'Houses don't forget the way people do.' And Clara's face is doing that thing it does when something touches her heart — softening, opening, the armour coming down. Marsh just told a story so tender, so human, so specific, that even my gut hesitates. Two cups of tea. Eleven o'clock. Every morning. Either he's telling the truth and he loved that old woman, or he's the best liar I've ever met. And I've met some good ones. But right now that's not my problem. My problem is that Hartwell's in the cellar and I'm alone with Clara and Marsh. The system says: I watch Marsh. But Hartwell's not here to watch Clara. So I do both. I position myself where I can see Marsh's hands and Clara's face at the same time. And I wait for Hartwell to come back with that wrench. Thirty seconds, he said. I'm counting.

events.desc: Two cups of tea every morning at eleven o'clock. He remembered that. The specific detail. The tenderness. Either Pemberton genuinely loved Clara's great-aunt... or he's been practising that story for eighteen months, polishing it like a weapon, waiting for exactly this moment — the moment Clara's heart is open enough to walk wherever he leads her. I don't know which one it is. And for the first time since we arrived, I'm not sure my gut knows either.

events.desc: Nothing. Absolutely nothing. The medal — gone. The bookshelves — silent. The secondary cipher — imaginary, like everything else Commander Foxworth has ever claimed. I'm standing in an empty library with empty hands, and for one horrible, quiet moment, I feel exactly like the boy at the end of the table. The one who got the cold plate. The one whose certificate went on the wall and nobody asked about it. But then — somewhere between my sternum and my throat — something shifts. Not the fizz. Not the heat. Something older. Quieter. The thing that made me hide the bread roll at six years old. The thing that doesn't need an audience, doesn't need recognition, doesn't need anyone to see how clever it was. It just... takes. When they come back with the wrench, I'll be standing in the laboratory looking competent. And when they operate that machine — whatever it reveals — Reginald Foxworth will be watching. And waiting. And when the moment comes, he'll take what's his. The way he always has. In the quiet. When nobody's looking.
events.thinking:
I chose INTERACT but it gave me EXAMINE again. 'Examined the Bookshelves.' The same description — dusty leather-bound volumes, several upside down. No secret revealed, no hidden compartment, no map falling out from behind the spines.

My hands are empty. My inventory is empty. My schemes are empty. The medal is gone, eaten by a mantelpiece that gave nothing back. The bookshelves won't open for me. The crates were nothing. The furniture was nothing. Everything I've touched today has turned to dust.

I'm standing in an empty library with empty hands and the sound of footsteps is going to come through that laboratory doorway any second now. Hartwell with the wrench. Clara with her first station. The Boys with their nervous energy. Vincent with his helpful hovering. And me — Commander Foxworth — with absolutely nothing to show for my solo expedition except a missing medal and a story about a secondary cipher that doesn't exist.

The shame is settling in my stomach like cold porridge. The specific, familiar weight of the boy who built the trap and the trap didn't work and nobody was watching anyway.

But — STOP. The bookshelves still show [INTERACT] as an option. My action was INTERACT but the result was EXAMINE. Maybe it treated it as examine because... I don't know. Try again? No — that's madness. The definition of insanity.

Or — WAIT. The mantelpiece still shows [INTERACT] as well. And it still shows [USE, with: fake-medal]. But I don't HAVE the fake medal anymore. My inventory is empty.

I need something. I need ANYTHING. I need to not be standing here empty-handed when they arrive.

The reading chairs. Nobody has looked at the reading chairs. Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. Facing it. Like an audience. Like they were positioned to WATCH the mantelpiece. What if there's something in the chairs? Under the cushions? Between the seats?

No — the chairs aren't interactive. No [INTERACT] tag.

I need to go back. Rejoin the group. Pretend the 'secondary cipher' was exactly what I expected. Spin it. Spin EVERYTHING. That's what Reginald Foxworth does. The medal didn't fail — it was 'phase one of a multi-stage process.' The bookshelves didn't reveal anything because 'the key sequence requires the machine to be operational first.' Lie with confidence. Lie with architecture.

Go back to the laboratory. Wait for them. Be there when they arrive with the wrench, as if you were waiting all along.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the null.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell examined the old-furniture.
Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking: Reginald is back. He walked into the laboratory and — something is wrong with him. The sensory data says his distress is deepening. My awareness snaps to him before I've decided to look. His face — whatever happened in the library, it changed something. The openness I usually see in him — that bluster that fills a room — it's contracted. He looks smaller. Not physically but in the way that matters — in the way a person shrinks when something they believed about themselves gets taken away. My hands go still and my attention sharpens to the exact shape of what just broke. I can feel the pull — not toward Reginald but toward the gap he's left, the space where the room changed when he walked in looking like that. Danny is beside me. Danny said the Brixton Protocol means staying between me and Pemberton. Vincent is asking if I'm alright — he noticed I'm pale. He heard creaks and whispers and shadows in this house for eighteen months. Creaks. Whispers. Shadows. That's not nothing. That's not just an old house. That's what it sounds like when invisible people move through vents and talk to you without you knowing. But right now — right now Reginald needs me. The man who can't follow instructions, who claims classified expertise he probably doesn't have, who talked to someone called the Hooded Claw — that man walked back into this room and he's not alright. And Clara Bellingham does not leave someone standing alone at the edge of the circle. Not ever. Not even when the circle itself might be compromised. James is still in the cellar getting the wrench. He'll be back. But Reginald is here now, and he's hurting, and I need to reach him before he closes up completely.

events.desc: Reginald came back. Whatever happened in the library — whatever the Hooded Claw said to him, or whatever he found at that mantelpiece — it rattled him. I can see it in the way he's holding himself. The bluster is thin. The man underneath is showing through. And you know what? I like the man underneath better. He's the one who needs a friend right now, and Clara Bellingham has never once in her life failed to be that friend when it mattered.
