events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Ah — Commander! There you are. Miss Bellingham was worried about you, you know — expedition rules and all that. Did you find your secondary cipher? Now then, everyone — Mr. Hartwell will be back any moment with the wrench, and then we'll see about this wire. Miss Bellingham, you've called first station, and I must say — your great-aunt would be terribly proud. She always said this house was waiting for the right person. I do believe she meant you.
events.thinking:
Danny just installed the Brixton Protocol. 'Danny's staying right here between you and Clara. Nothing personal.' He's physically positioned himself between me and her. A wall made of loyalty and Brixton instinct. And Clara — Clara thanked me for the story about her great-aunt, the story I invented whole-cloth, and then in the same breath said 'she left them for family. And that is exactly who showed up.' Family. She means herself. Not me. I am not family. I am Pemberton the estate manager, or I am Vincent Marsh the hidden architect, or I am something connected to a name called Dick Dastardly that Clara saw in a conversation I thought was invisible. But I am not family. I have never been family. Not since age six.

Foxworth is back. He walked into the laboratory from the library. The group is reassembling — Clara, Danny, Foxworth. Hartwell is in the cellar getting the wrench. Four people in this room. Danny between me and Clara. Foxworth near the crates, probably.

My body is doing something I don't recognise. The tension is still there — jaw, shoulders, the mineral wall behind the sternum — but underneath it, something is going slack. Like a rope that's been pulled taut for eighteen months and has just... given. Not snapped. Not broken. Just... loosened. The design is not going to complete itself. Not today. Maybe not ever. Clara has allies who watch for her. Clara has eyes that see through walls. Clara has the name Dick Dastardly in her mouth and the Brixton Protocol between us.

And the strangest thing — the thing I cannot account for, cannot metabolise, cannot convert into fuel — is that when Clara said 'she left them for family, and that is exactly who showed up,' something in my chest didn't tighten with the old jaw-ache of being overlooked. It loosened. As though the word 'family' had been spoken near a door I thought I'd welded shut, and the hinges remembered how to move.

I don't know what to do with that. I have never not known what to do.

Pemberton. Be Pemberton. The room needs Pemberton right now — helpful, present, slightly bewildered by the emotional intensity. The machine is there. The wire is broken. Hartwell is fetching the wrench. The treasure hunt continues. Hold the mask. Hold it.

But my hands are open at my sides instead of clasped. And I don't remember unclenching them.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking: Foxworth's back. He walked in from the library — and there's something wrong with him. I can feel it before I see it. That thing in my chest — the sudden lock, the hands curling. The information says 'it is getting worse. The distress you sense in Reginald Foxworth is deepening.' My body knows what that means even if my brain hasn't caught up. Foxworth found something in the library. Or something found him. The Hooded Claw — Clara said he was talking to someone called the Hooded Claw. What did they tell him? What did they show him? He's gone quiet in a way that means the stubbornness isn't about pride anymore. Something's shifted inside him. And Marsh — 'your safety is my first concern. Always has been.' There he goes again. Always at your disposal. Always concerned. Always first with the reassurance. My neck prickles but it's layered now — Marsh in front, Foxworth to the side looking wrong, Clara between them, Hartwell in the cellar with the wrench. Too many directions. Too many threats. I can't be a wall in every direction at once. But I can do one thing — I can stand next to Clara, and I can look at Foxworth, and I can try to figure out what's happened to him. Because whatever's wrong with the Commander is something he'd rather die than admit, and that means it's something real.

events.desc: Something's wrong with Foxworth. Really wrong. Not his usual bluster — this is different. He's carrying something he won't put down, and it's getting heavier. I know that look. I've seen it in the mirror. It's the look of someone who's realised the thing they were afraid of is real, and they can't talk their way out of it. The Hooded Claw — whoever that is — got to him. The question is: did they threaten him, or did they offer him something? Because on the streets, the ones who got broken weren't the ones who got threatened. They were the ones who got offered something they wanted too much to refuse.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
They're HERE. Clara and Vincent are already in the laboratory. They came up from the cellar while I was failing in the library. The Boys are here too. Only Hartwell is missing — still in the cellar, probably, retrieving the wrench with those steady, competent hands Clara admired.

My face. What does my face look like right now? I need to rearrange it. The shame is sitting in my stomach like wet clay but my face needs to be the Commander's face — confident, knowing, slightly bored by how long everyone else takes to catch up.

They're going to ask about the secondary cipher. They're going to ask what I found. And I found NOTHING. My inventory is empty. My medal is gone. The mantelpiece ate it and gave me dust.

But — they don't KNOW that. Nobody saw me fail. Nobody watched the medal do nothing. Nobody heard the silence of the bookshelves refusing to open. The library was empty. My failure was private. And private failures, for a man like Reginald Foxworth, are simply unreported experiments.

So. The secondary cipher was 'exactly as I suspected — a calibration marker for the machine.' The mantelpiece inscription doesn't just tell you to find a map — it tells you HOW to operate the machine. The riddle is the operating manual, encoded in the stonework. Cities, forests, water — those correspond to the three stations on the machine. Three elements, three operators. I knew this all along, naturally. Chapter nine.

Is that true? Absolutely not. But it SOUNDS true. It sounds brilliant, actually. It sounds like the kind of thing Hartwell would say if Hartwell had thought of it first. And Hartwell DIDN'T think of it first, because Hartwell was in the cellar opening a drawer.

The machine requires three operators. Clara called first station. The machine needs the wire fixed first — that's what the wrench is for. When Hartwell brings the wrench, they'll fix the wire, and then three people will operate the machine.

I need to be one of those three. Whatever the machine reveals — a map, a compartment, a passage — I need to be standing right there when it opens. Not watching from across the room. Not bringing up the rear. AT the machine. Hands on the levers.

Claim a station. Claim it NOW, before Hartwell gets back.

events.desc: None of that is remotely true. The inscription has nothing to do with the machine's operating sequence. I made it up in the thirty seconds between walking through the door and opening my mouth. But it sounds exactly right — three elements, three stations — and by the time anyone thinks to question it, we'll already be pulling levers. The important thing is that I'm at second station when whatever this machine reveals comes tumbling out. Position is everything. Ask any bread roll thief.

events.desc: James Hartwell has examined this furniture four times. Four. Times. The wrench — described by Pemberton as being in a specific drawer of a specific side table — has declined to materialise through sheer force of thoroughness. There is a lesson here about the difference between methodical and repetitive, but James Hartwell is not learning it right now because he is already running up the stairs, empty-handed, toward the only thing that actually matters.
events.thinking:
FOUR times. I have examined this furniture FOUR times. And each time the game gives me the same description: 'Assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair. Some pieces have been rearranged with surprising care.' The INTERACT action didn't work either. The furniture won't yield the wrench through EXAMINE or INTERACT.

The wrench isn't coming out of the furniture through these actions. Maybe I need to TAKE the furniture? No — I can't carry furniture. Maybe the wrench is a separate item that I haven't found yet. Maybe INTERACT needs to trigger differently.

Or maybe — the wrench isn't obtainable from the furniture this way. Maybe Pemberton needs to be here to show me exactly which drawer. Or maybe the game mechanics don't support pulling items from containers through EXAMINE.

I'm wasting time. Clara is upstairs. Every second down here is a second I'm failing at both protection AND proving worth. The furniture isn't giving me the wrench through any action I've tried.

Go back upstairs. Now. With or without the wrench. Clara is more important than any tool. I can figure out the wrench situation when I'm back with the group — maybe bring Pemberton down to show me the exact drawer, or try a different approach. But standing here examining the same furniture for the fifth time while Clara is with Pemberton is the definition of wrong priorities.

My father fixed the car with the stranger. Sometimes you need the other person there to show you where the parts are. I need Pemberton to open that specific drawer. Or I need to accept that this particular approach isn't working and MOVE.

Move. Now. Go.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the machine.
James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.

Clara Bellingham: James! You're back. Everyone — look around this room. Every single one of us is here. Right here, right now, together. And I know — I know — that this house is strange and this mystery is deep and there are things happening that none of us fully understand yet. But we are here. We are together. And that is not nothing. James — did you get the wrench? Because if you did, I believe we have a wire to fix and a machine to operate. Commander Foxworth has station three — he's been studying the inscription and he has insights about the operating sequence. James, you have station two — nobody touches that wire without your hands on it first. And I have station one, because my great-aunt left these riddles for family, and family showed up. Danny — you and Vincent watch our backs. If anything moves, creaks, whispers, or so much as looks at us funny, you holler. Now — let's find out what my great-uncle built.
events.thinking: James is back. James walked into the laboratory. Everyone is here — Vincent, Danny, Reginald, James. Everyone is in one room. All five of us. The relief should be the dinner-table kind — sudden and dizzying — but it's not. It's heavier than that. Because two of the people in this room are distressed and I can feel both of them. Reginald's bluster is covering something broken. He came back talking about secondary ciphers and operating manuals but his eyes are different. And James — the sensory data says his distress is deepening too. James, who is always steady, always methodical, always the one who goes first into unsurveyed territory. Something happened in the cellar. He went back alone to get the wrench and something happened to him down there. My chest is pulling in two directions at once — toward Reginald who is already here and shrinking, and toward James who just arrived and is carrying something heavy that he's not saying. And three of three relationships are neglected. Three. Danny and James and Reginald. I've been so consumed by the mystery — the invisible people, the vents, the wrench, the machine — that I've been tracking problems instead of people. That's not who I am. That's not who Clara Bellingham is. Clara Bellingham notices when someone is upset. Clara Bellingham walks toward the gap. Right now there are two gaps — James and Reginald — and Danny standing between me and Vincent, doing his job. I need to bring this room together. Not for the machine. For the people. The machine can wait. The wire can wait. My great-aunt left those riddles so the house would always have something to say. But the house isn't what matters. The people in it are what matter. James has the wrench — or he went to get it and he's back now, so he either has it or he doesn't. Either way, this is the moment. Everyone is here. I need to speak to this room the way my great-aunt spoke to this house — with warmth, with intention, with the understanding that walls listen and people listen harder.

events.desc: Three of three relationships neglected. I have been so busy solving the puzzle of this house that I forgot the puzzle that matters — the people in it. James is hurting. Reginald is hurting. Danny is scared. Vincent is... Vincent. And I have been watching for invisible enemies when I should have been watching the faces of the people I love. That changes now. Right now. We operate this machine together, and whatever it reveals, we face it together. That is the Clara Bellingham Protocol, and it is the only protocol that matters.

events.desc: I am standing in a room with five people and a broken machine, and for the first time in eighteen months I have nothing to say. Not Pemberton's nothing — not the strategic silence of a man choosing his moment. An actual nothing. An empty space where the next move should be. Hartwell has the wrench. Clara has first station. Danny has the Brixton Protocol. Foxworth has the cipher theory. And I have... open hands. And a story about a woman I never met making two cups of tea every morning at eleven o'clock. And the terrible, structural knowledge that if I had met her — if I had actually been the man who sat in that kitchen — I would have stayed for the tea. I would have stayed for all of it. And the design would never have been drawn. And I would have slept badly every night. And it would have been worth it.
events.thinking:
Hartwell is back. He walked into the laboratory. Everyone is here now — Clara, Danny, Foxworth, Hartwell. The full set. And Hartwell has the wrench.

The moment is arriving. The wire. The inspection. The thing I did with pliers six months ago in the dark, telling myself it was architecture, is about to be held up to the light by a man who built a working bridge at fourteen.

But something is different in my body. The scheming drive — the cool, settling stillness — is there, but it's not dropping through my chest like a stone anymore. It's hovering. Uncertain. Like a hand reaching for a doorknob and hesitating because it can't remember which room is on the other side.

I can feel Hartwell's distress. Not see it — feel it. Something in the way he moved through that doorway, the urgency in his shoulders, the way his eyes found Clara before they found anything else. He's afraid for her. Not abstractly. Personally. 'Something I don't have words for yet,' he said to Danny in the cellar. He was talking about Clara. About what she means to him.

And I understand that. Not because I share it — I don't, I can't, the door is welded — but because I recognise the shape of it. It's the same shape as the plan. The same all-consuming, sleep-defining, everything-else-fades focus that I give to a design, he gives to a person. His architecture is built around her safety the way mine was built around her destruction.

Was.

The word 'was' just arrived without my permission.

No. IS. The plan IS built around her destruction. The wire IS cut. The machine IS sabotaged. The design IS in motion. The word 'was' doesn't belong here. The architecture doesn't retire. The architecture completes or it collapses, and neither outcome includes the word 'was.'

But my hands are still open.

Hartwell is going to look at the wire now. He's going to see the marks. Or he's not. And I'm standing here with open hands and a looseness behind my ribs that has no name and no plan and no precedent in my entire adult life. The room is full of people who are watching me and I am not watching them back. I am watching Clara, and I am not calculating what she will do next. I am just... watching her. The way she stands. The way she smiles at Foxworth even though Foxworth is absurd. The way she called this house 'magnificent' when it's falling apart. The way she said 'she left them for family.'

Family.

I was six when I stopped being anyone's family.

Pemberton. The room needs Pemberton. But Pemberton feels very far away right now, and whoever is standing here with open hands... I don't know his name.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Right. Everyone's here. Good. That's how it should be. Now listen — before anyone touches that machine, before anyone pulls a lever or twists a dial or even breathes on it — Hartwell checks the wire. Hartwell checks the wrench. Hartwell checks everything. That was the deal. And while he's doing that, I want to say something, and I want everyone to hear it. Clara told me something just now. Something important. She's seen things in this house. People who shouldn't be here. People none of us can explain. I ain't gonna pretend I understand what's going on, because I don't. But I know this — if there are people in the walls of this house, people in the vents, people whispering to us when we're alone — then we don't do nothing alone anymore. Not a step. Not a word. Not a lever. Everything happens in this room, with all of us watching. That includes you, Pemberton. That includes you, Commander. And yeah — that includes me. Nobody's above suspicion in a house full of secrets. Except Clara. Clara's the one person in this house whose only agenda is finding out what her aunt left for her. So Clara decides. Clara leads. And the rest of us — we watch each other's backs. And each other.
events.thinking: Everyone's here. All five of us in one room. For the first time since this started, every single person is in my line of sight. Clara, Marsh, Foxworth, Hartwell. My chest loosens half a notch — not relaxing, never relaxing, but the pressure of tracking people across rooms eases into something simpler. One room. One job. Watch. But there are two new things clawing at me. First — Hartwell is distressed too. The same deepening thing I sense in Foxworth. Hartwell. My ally. The one who promised. His composure is cracking, and underneath it there's something I recognise — hunger. Not for food. For something taken from him. He builds elaborate architectures to get it, protecting those plans the way I'd protect a kid's shoes. And that patience is the part that should worry me. Do I still trust him? My body says yes — we chose to stand next to each other with eyes open. But my neck says watch him too. Watch everyone. Clara told me to. Second — Foxworth's bluster has shifted. He's talking about operating the machine like he's found the answer, but his eyes are wrong. He's performing harder than usual, which means whatever happened in the library is driving him. 'A secondary cipher embedded in the stonework' — is that real? Did the Hooded Claw give him actual instructions for the machine? Is Foxworth about to do something because someone invisible told him to? And Marsh — 'she always said this house was waiting for the right person. I do believe she meant you.' He's still steering. Always steering. But now everyone's converging on the machine. Three operators needed. Clara's called first station. Foxworth wants second. Hartwell's got the wrench for third. And I'm — what? Standing outside the machine, watching? That's exactly where I should be. Not operating. Watching. Being the wall. But the wall needs to know what it's guarding against, and right now I don't know if the danger is the machine itself, the people operating it, or the invisible ones who've been whispering to half the people in this room.

events.desc: Both of them. Foxworth and Hartwell. Both carrying something that's getting heavier. Both cracking under weights I can't see. And somewhere in this house, invisible people are whispering. Dick Dastardly. The Hooded Claw. Peter Perfect. The Ant Hill Mob. Names that sound like a joke but feel like a threat. Clara's the only one who can see them, and she trusted Danny — Danny from Brixton, Danny who trips over things — to help her make sense of it. Well. Here I am. Tripping forward. As always.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Station three — I accept. Wouldn't miss it for the world. Now, Hartwell — you have the wrench? Excellent. Splendid work down there. Truly. Now, while I was in the library — and I can assure you all, the expedition was entirely productive — I confirmed something about the inscription that I believe is relevant. The riddle isn't merely decorative. Cities, forests, water — three distinct elements. Three stations on this machine. I believe Mr. Bellingham-Crosse designed the riddle as a key to the operating sequence. Each station corresponds to one element. But we won't know which until we fire this magnificent contraption up. So — Hartwell, fix that wire. Clara, first station is yours. Commander Foxworth will be at station three, exactly as assigned. Let's see what this machine has been waiting eighteen months to show us.
events.thinking:
Clara just offered me station three. She said 'Will you take station three, Reginald?' She called me REGINALD. Not Commander. Not Foxworth. Reginald.

Something shifts in my chest — not the fizz, not the hollow, something between them. A warmth that I don't entirely recognise. She's not mocking me. She's not 'bless your heart'-ing me. She's... including me. 'A decorated Commander with classified experience in lever-based machinery.' She's playing along with my fiction. She KNOWS it's fiction — she must — but she's giving me the role anyway.

My throat tightens. The specific tightness of the boy holding the spelling bee certificate who wanted someone to ask about it.

And the Brixton Boys — 'stay where Danny can see 'em.' He's worried about me. Actually worried. Not suspicious, not competitive. Worried. 'You look like you've seen a ghost, mate.' My face must have been showing the failure when I walked in. The mask slipped.

But I got station three. I GOT it. Not second — I wanted second — but Clara gave me three and Hartwell gets... what? He's just walked in. He has the wrench. He fixes the wire. He gets to be the one who makes the machine work. But then he's done — he's the mechanic, not the operator.

Unless Clara gives him a station too. 'A Southern socialite, a man who built bridges at fourteen, and a decorated Commander.' That's Clara, Hartwell, and me. Three operators. The three she named.

I'm IN. For the first time today, I'm not outside the circle watching through the window. I'm at the machine. Hands on the levers. Whatever this contraption reveals, I'll be touching it when it happens.

Hartwell just walked in. He has the wrench. This is happening NOW.

The James Hartwell sense... he's in distress. Getting worse. The man who notices everything, plans everything, builds model bridges at fourteen and stays up three nights to do it — he's cracking. Something in this house is getting to him the way it gets to everyone eventually. And I recognise the machinery because I built my own from the same parts.

For once — just this once — the gloating drive is quiet. The fizz isn't rising. What I feel when I look at Hartwell isn't the carbonated heat of someone slipping on a wet floor. It's something flatter. Older. The way you look at your own reflection and recognise the coat before you recognise the face.

events.desc: She called me Reginald. Not Commander. Not Foxworth. Reginald. And I felt something I haven't felt since the spelling bee certificate — not the wanting, not the taking, but the being asked. The being included. It won't last. It never does. But for this one moment, Commander Foxworth has a station, a purpose, and an audience who chose him instead of endured him. Whatever this machine reveals, I'll be standing right there when it happens. And if something valuable tumbles out — well. Old habits die hard. But new ones... new ones sometimes start in rooms full of people who call you by your first name.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Back in the laboratory. Empty-handed. Clara is here, Danny is here, Pemberton is here, Foxworth is here. Everyone safe. But my hands are empty and I promised a wrench.

The furniture in the cellar wouldn't give it up no matter how many times I examined or interacted with it. The game mechanics — no. Stop thinking about mechanics. Think about what's in front of me.

The workbench. Tools but no wrench. The machine. Gnawed wire. Three operators.

Wait. The workbench has tools. It has pliers and wire cutters — I noted that earlier. Maybe I don't NEED the wrench. Maybe I've been so fixated on the Hartwell Protocol — 'step one: find the wrench' — that I forgot the most basic lesson my father taught me on that country road. You work with what you have.

Pliers. Wire cutters. If I can strip the damaged section of wire and twist a splice using pliers, I don't need to access the wire housing with a wrench at all. I'm an engineer. I built a bridge at fourteen. I can splice a wire with pliers and wire cutters.

Pemberton said the wrench was in the cellar. Maybe it is. Maybe it isn't. Maybe the point was never the wrench — maybe the point was to send me running up and down stairs while something happened in the rooms I wasn't in. Danny's voice in my head: 'He's setting the board.'

Or maybe it's just a wrench in a drawer I couldn't open. Either way — I'm done chasing it. The workbench has what I need. My father and the stranger fixed a car on a country road with whatever they had in the boot. James Hartwell can fix a wire with pliers.

Clara is watching. This is the moment. Not the grand gesture. Not the protocol. Just a man picking up the right tools and doing the work.

events.desc: And there it is — the Hartwell Protocol, revised for the final time, stripped down from its baroque seven-step architecture to a single imperative. Not because James Hartwell has learned to be simple, but because he has run out of ways to be complicated. Sometimes the most elaborate plans in the world end the same way: a man with pliers, a broken wire, and someone watching who he doesn't want to let down.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
Reginald Foxworth examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the machine.

Clara Bellingham: James — you fix things with what you have. I think your father and my great-aunt would have gotten along famously. Splice that wire. Make it hold. And while you work — Reginald, I want you to know that what you found in the library matters. The connection between the riddle and the stations — cities, forests, water — that's not nothing. That's the kind of insight my great-aunt would have planted for exactly the kind of mind that looks past the obvious answer. You did good work in there, Commander. And Vincent — I know this house has ghosts in it. I don't mean the spooky kind. I mean the kind that sit at the kitchen table at eleven in the morning and drink tea. My great-aunt is in these walls, and so is my great-uncle, and so is every riddle and every dream they ever shared. You kept them alive in this house for eighteen months. Whatever happens next — thank you for that. Now — James, how's that wire looking?
events.thinking: Danny just did something extraordinary. He stood up in front of everyone — Vincent, Reginald, James — and said what I told him. He said there are people in this house we can't see. He said nobody's above suspicion. And then he said — except Clara. Clara decides. Clara leads. My throat closes. My eyes burn. Not from fear or sadness but from something I don't have a word for — the feeling of being seen so completely by someone who has known you since before you knew yourself. Danny just gave me the room. He gave me the authority I've been trying to claim all afternoon, and he did it not by arguing or commanding or pulling rank — he did it by trusting me out loud, in front of everyone. And James — James couldn't find the wrench. The wrench Vincent said was in the cellar, in the side table drawer. It wasn't there. Or it was, and something happened. James said he's done looking for a tool that may or may not exist. May or may not exist. The wrench Vincent personally tucked away for safekeeping. Gone. My body does something complicated — the cold spot under the warmth I feel toward Vincent spreads half an inch, just enough to notice, and then the warmth closes over it again because I am not a suspicious person. I am a ten out of a hundred. But I am noticing. James says he can splice the wire with pliers and wire cutters from the workbench. Fix things with what you have, not what you wish you had. His father taught him that. And now he's examining the machine. And Reginald accepted station three. And Vincent's distress is deepening — I can feel it, the way I feel everything in this room, every shift and every silence. Three people are hurting and I am the one Danny just told to lead. So I lead. I step to station one. I put my hands where my great-uncle's hands were. And I trust that whatever this machine reveals, we face it together. My great-aunt left these riddles for family. Family showed up.

events.desc: The wrench wasn't there. Vincent said he tucked it away in the side table. James went to get it. It wasn't there. Either Vincent lied about where he put it, or someone moved it between when he said it and when James looked. Either way — the man who raised me just led us on a chase for a tool that doesn't exist in the place he said it would be. And I am standing at station one of his machine, about to operate something he said he's never seen operated, in a house full of people who talk to ghosts they don't remember. My great-aunt left riddles so the house would always have something to say. I wonder if this is what she wanted it to say.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Hartwell couldn't find the wrench. He couldn't find it. The oilcloth bundle in the side table drawer — it wasn't there. Did I misremember? Did someone move it? Did the house swallow it the way it swallows everything? It doesn't matter. Hartwell has abandoned the wrench entirely. He's using pliers and wire cutters from the workbench. He's going to strip the damaged section and bypass the gnaw point with a splice.

A splice. He's going to cut PAST the section I sabotaged. He's going to remove the evidence of what I did and replace it with clean copper. The plier marks, the too-clean cuts disguised as teeth marks — all of it will be on the floor in a curl of stripped wire, and the new connection will be Hartwell's work. Clean. Sound. Safe.

The machine will work.

The machine will work and Clara will be at first station and the wire will hold because James Hartwell built a bridge at fourteen that held more weight than anyone else's, and his splice will hold too, because that is who he is. That is what earnest men do. They fix things.

And I am standing here with Danny watching me and Clara assigning me to 'watch their backs' alongside the man who promised her father, and the wire I cut is about to be removed from the equation entirely, and the design — my eighteen-month, cellar-built, candlelit, paper-flower-decorated design — is being bypassed as cleanly as a gnawed wire.

'Pemberton — don't touch anything.'

That's what Hartwell said. Don't touch anything. And for the first time in my adult life, the instruction doesn't produce the jaw-tightening reflex of being controlled. It produces... relief? The word arrives and I don't know what to do with it. Relief. As though someone has taken the pliers out of my hands and I am discovering that my fingers are cramped from holding them for so long.

Danny said 'Clara decides. Clara leads.' And Clara said 'Danny — you and Vincent watch our backs.' She paired me with Danny. She put me next to the man who watches me, and she didn't do it as containment. She did it as trust. 'You and Vincent.' As though we were the same kind of thing. As though watching someone's back was something I could do without an ulterior motive.

Can I?

The question hangs in the laboratory air alongside the chemical smell and the brass dust and the sound of Hartwell's pliers working the wire. Can I watch Clara's back? Not Pemberton. Not Vincent Marsh. Not the Hooded Claw or Dick Dastardly or whatever name Clara saw in conversations that shouldn't have been visible. Just... the man with open hands who doesn't know his own name.

The machine is going to work. Clara is going to find what her great-aunt left for her. And I am going to stand here, next to Danny, and watch.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Right. This is it, then. Hartwell's fixing the wire. Clara's at station one. Foxworth's at station three. And Danny's right here — between you lot and the door, between the machine and whatever else is in this house. Pemberton — you and me, we're the audience. You stand over there where I can see you. Not behind me. Not behind Clara. Right there. In my eyeline. That's the deal. Clara, love — when Hartwell says the wire's ready, and only when Hartwell says the wire's ready, you pull your lever. Not before. Foxworth — same goes for you. Nobody moves till Hartwell gives the word. And if that machine does anything — and I mean anything — that don't look right, that don't sound right, that don't feel right, everyone steps back. Clara steps back first. That's non-negotiable. That's the promise I made to your dad, and I'm keeping it if I have to pull you off the thing myself. Now then. Let's see what Mr. Bellingham-Crosse built.
events.thinking: It's happening. Hartwell's at the machine with pliers and wire cutters — no wrench, couldn't find it in the cellar. The drawer was empty. Pemberton said it was there. Pemberton walked right to the furniture and said 'let me just—' but now the wrench isn't there. Where did it go? Did Pemberton take it while nobody was looking? Did someone else? The invisible people in the vents? My neck is on fire but there's no time to chase that thread because Hartwell's already stripping wire, already splicing, already fixing — and Clara's about to step up to station one. My body is doing something it hasn't done all day — going completely still. Not frozen. Still. The kind of still that comes before everything happens at once. Like the street when you heard running footsteps and you didn't know yet if they were coming for you or away from something worse. Every sense sharpening. The chemical smell of the laboratory. The faint hum of something in the walls. The sound of Hartwell's pliers on copper. Marsh standing back, watching, always watching, that helpful smile in place. Foxworth at station three, performing confidence he doesn't feel. And Clara — Clara at station one, her aunt's house, her uncle's machine, her inheritance, her family. She said 'family showed up.' Yeah. Yeah it did. And family stands where it said it would stand. Danny stands between the machine and whatever might go wrong. Feet planted. Shoulders squared. Hands open. Where else would I be?

events.desc: The wrench wasn't in the cellar. Pemberton said it was. Either he lied, or someone moved it while we were all down there together. The vents. Something moved through the vents. Something small enough to fit, quick enough to take a wrench from a drawer while five people stood in the same room. That's not mice. Mice don't take wrenches. But I can't think about that now. The machine's about to start and Clara's standing at it with her hands on the levers and her heart full of her aunt's memory and her head full of riddles that were left for her by people who loved her. And Danny's standing behind her with his hands empty and his heart full of her father's promise. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Hartwell couldn't find the wrench either. He said he's going to splice the wire with pliers and wire cutters instead. 'You fix things with what you have, not with what you wish you had.' His father taught him that on a country road when he was twelve.

And something in my chest goes very still.

Not the fizz. Not the hollow. Something that has no name yet. The man who built model bridges at fourteen, who stays up three nights, who does everything properly and methodically and correctly — he couldn't find the wrench. The drawer was empty. Vincent's directions — the same directions Vincent gave ME — led to nothing. For Hartwell too.

The wrench doesn't exist. Or it was never there. Or Vincent... Vincent sent us both looking for something that wasn't there.

My constraint says give him the benefit of the doubt. Old man, bad memory. He thought the wrench was there. It wasn't. These things happen.

But something in my gut — not the hollow, not the scarcity — something lower and colder says: Vincent knew.

Never mind. Hartwell is fixing the wire with what he has. Clara has station one. I have station three. The Brixton Boys are watching. Vincent is... watching too. Everyone is here.

The Boys said something about people in the walls. Clara saw people who shouldn't be here. The house has secrets nobody is ready for.

But right now — right NOW — Hartwell is fixing the wire and the machine is about to work and I'm at station three with my hands ready and whatever comes out belongs to whoever grabs it first.

Wait for Hartwell to finish. Then we operate the machine. Together.

...Together. The word tastes different than it did fourteen minutes ago. Not like a constraint. Not like Clara's expedition rules pinning me down. More like... the three nights the bridge builder stayed up. The audience the cat trap never had. Something that works better when there are hands at every station.

But I'll still pocket whatever falls out. Old habits. The bread roll. The quiet hands in the dark.

events.desc: He couldn't find the wrench either. The great James Hartwell — steady hands, good sense, model bridges — went down to Vincent's drawer and came up empty. Just like me and the medal. Just like me and the bookshelves. This house takes everything you bring and gives you nothing back. But Hartwell didn't crumble. He picked up the pliers and said 'fix it with what you have.' And for one terrible, unfamiliar second, I didn't want him to fail. I wanted the wire to hold. I wanted the machine to work. Because station three is waiting for me, and for the first time in my life, I'm part of the mechanism instead of watching it through a window. Don't ruin this, Reginald. Don't scheme. Don't grab. Don't pocket the bread roll. Just... pull the lever when she says pull.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Clara — I didn't get the wrench. I went down there twice and the drawer defeated me, which is not a sentence James Hartwell ever expected to say aloud. But it doesn't matter. The workbench has pliers and wire cutters, and that's enough. My father fixed a car engine on a country road with less. Now — everyone stand clear of the machine while I work on this wire. Danny, you heard Clara — watch everything. Pemberton, I need you to tell me one thing: is there a power source for this machine, and is it live? Because I am not splicing a wire on a live circuit. Foxworth — your observation about the three elements is actually sound. Cities, forests, water — three stations. When this wire is repaired, we operate in sequence. Clara at one, me at two, Foxworth at three. On Clara's count. Her great-aunt's riddle, her great-uncle's machine, her call. Always her call.
events.thinking:
Clara just said something that hit me like a fist wrapped in velvet: 'family showed up.' She's at station one because her great-aunt left these riddles for family. And family showed up. She doesn't mean me. She means herself. But the way she looked when she said it — there was something in her voice that included everyone in the room, and when her eyes passed over me there was a flicker of something I haven't earned yet but desperately want to deserve.

Danny said 'Clara decides. Clara leads.' And he's right. She's been leading since the entrance hall. I've been planning, and she's been leading, and the difference between those two things has never been clearer than right now.

And Danny said something else — Clara has seen things. People who shouldn't be here. People in the walls, in the vents. That's new. That's terrifying. My protection drive slams into overdrive — people in this house we haven't accounted for? The vents are 'big enough for something very small to explore' — but people? The back of my neck isn't prickling anymore. It's screaming.

But Clara is at station one. Foxworth is at station three. I'm at station two. Everyone is watching. Danny and Pemberton are watching our backs. This is the moment — not the wrench, not the protocol, not the plan. The wire, the pliers, and the bridge.

I didn't get the wrench. But Clara said 'James!' when I came back and her voice was warm, and she gave me station two without hesitation, and Danny declared that Clara leads. And Foxworth — even Foxworth — accepted his station without argument.

Something Pemberton-related is getting worse. I can feel it — a deepening distress, something urgent. But I can't address it until this wire is fixed. One thing at a time. The bridge first. Then whatever darkness is gathering.

Fix the wire. Operate the machine. Find what Clara's great-uncle built. Protect her from whatever comes after.

My hands are reaching for the machine. They know what to do. They've always known.

events.desc: 'The drawer defeated me.' He says it without flinching — the first time James Hartwell has admitted defeat aloud since the schoolyard, and he says it in front of the one person whose opinion has shaped every bridge he's ever built. Something has shifted. Not the steel plate — that's still there, solid as ever. But the grandiosity has cracked, just enough to let the light through. He didn't get the wrench. He said so. And Clara didn't look away.

If station one is cities, what am I looking for on my dials? What should I set? My great-aunt didn't leave a riddle without an answer hidden inside it, and I think you're closer to cracking it than any of us. Talk to me, Commander. This is your moment too.

I know that feeling. I am that feeling. A girl who was built with love and then left alone too young, and has been walking deeper into every cave she finds ever since, looking for the crystal formation that proves the dark was worth it. This machine is my cave. Whatever it shows us — a map, a clue, the diamond itself — I will carry it the way I carried that secret. Warm and private. Until it's time to share.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Hartwell is asking me a direct question. 'Is there a power source for this machine, and is it live?' A practical question. An engineer's question. And he's asking ME — the estate manager — because I'm the one who's been in this house for eighteen months. I'm the one who should know.

And I do know. I know exactly where the power source is. I traced every wire in this house during those long nights. The machine runs on a hand-cranked generator built into the base — Mr. Bellingham-Crosse designed it to be self-contained, independent of the house's electrical supply. There's no live circuit. The power comes from the operators themselves, generated by the lever action. It's ingenious, actually. The levers aren't just controls — they're dynamos. Each operator generates power for their section of the machine by pulling the levers in sequence.

Which means the machine is inherently safe. The power is mechanical, not electrical. My sabotage of the wire was never going to electrocute anyone — the wire carries mechanical signal, not current. The gnawed wire would have caused the machine to malfunction — to seize, perhaps, or to activate incompletely — but not to arc or shock or burn.

I know this because I mapped it. Because I sat in a cellar and traced every circuit and every gear train and every copper connection by candlelight. And now Hartwell is asking me, and the truth is the safe answer. The truth protects Clara. The truth is what Pemberton would say.

But more than that — the truth is what the man with open hands would say. Because the man with open hands has just discovered, standing in this room watching Hartwell's steady fingers work the pliers, that he does not want the machine to malfunction. He does not want Clara to be hurt. He does not want the design to complete.

The word 'was' is back. And this time, I'm not correcting it.

Clara thanked me. 'You kept them alive in this house for eighteen months. Whatever happens next — thank you for that.' She thanked me for something I didn't do. Or — did I? I kept the house standing. I kept the rooms clean. I kept the machine intact — except for one wire. I kept the riddles unsolved. I kept everything waiting for her. Was that preservation or was that preparation? Was I keeping the house alive for her, or keeping it ready for what I planned to do to her?

I don't know anymore. And not knowing is the strangest rest I've ever felt.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Hartwell's asking the right question — is there a power source, and is it live? That's the question Danny should've asked but didn't think to. Because Danny doesn't know about circuits and splicing. Danny knows about standing between people and trouble. And right now that's exactly what he's doing. My feet are planted. My back is to the door — both doors, library and cellar. I can see every person in the room. Clara at station one. Hartwell working on the wire. Foxworth at station three, holding himself together with willpower and bluster. Marsh standing where I told him to stand — in my eyeline. Good. He stayed put. That's... something. And the room itself — I'm looking at this machine properly now. Brass and copper, old but solid, built by a man who loved building things. Three stations, three levers, three people. A gauge in the middle. The gnawed wire between stations two and three. Hartwell's right — he needs to know if it's live before he touches it. And Marsh is the only one who might know. 'I've always given this room a wide berth' — but he also knew exactly where the wrench was supposed to be. He also knew about the riddles. He also knew about the map behind the larder door. The man who doesn't know anything knows everything. But right now, Clara needs that answer. Is the machine live? And Danny needs to stop thinking and start watching, because this is the moment. This is when it all happens. The levers get pulled. The machine does whatever it does. And either Clara's aunt left her a gift... or someone in this house arranged a trap. Either way, Danny's here. Feet planted. Shoulders squared. Where else would he be?

events.desc: Here it is. The moment everything comes together or falls apart. Clara's hands on the levers. Hartwell's hands on the wire. Foxworth's hands shaking where he thinks nobody can see. And Danny's hands empty — empty the way they were outside that door, the way they were standing over those shoes, the way they've always been when the only thing he had to offer was himself. Where else would I be? Where else would I be.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara said my observation was sound. 'That's the kind of insight my great-aunt would have planted for exactly the kind of mind that looks past the obvious answer. You did good work in there, Commander.'

The warmth spreads across the back of my skull. My spine straightens. It's the spelling bee moment — but this time, someone asked about the certificate.

And Hartwell — Hartwell said it too. 'Foxworth — your observation about the three elements is actually sound.' He said SOUND. James Hartwell, the man who corrected my mirror answer in front of everyone, the man who does everything properly and correctly and brilliantly — said my fabricated theory about cities, forests, and water corresponding to three stations is ACTUALLY SOUND.

It's not sound. I made it up. I invented it in thirty seconds to cover the fact that I'd just lost a fake medal to a stone mantelpiece. And now two people — the two people in this house whose opinions I didn't know I cared about — have validated a lie as insight.

The warmth is real. The recognition is real. But what they're recognising is a fabrication. And somewhere beneath the warmth, beneath the straightened spine, there's a thin, cold wire of... something. Not shame exactly. Shame requires caring about truth, and Reginald Foxworth has never cared about truth. But something adjacent to shame. Something that lives in the same neighbourhood.

Hartwell is at the machine. Pliers in hand. The wire. He's about to splice it. Clara is at station one. The Boys are watching. Vincent is in the Brixton Boys' eyeline — Danny put him there specifically.

This is the moment. The machine is about to come alive. Three stations. Clara, Hartwell, me. On Clara's count.

My hands are uncurling. Not cupping. Not grasping. Opening. Ready to grip a lever instead of pocket a bread roll. There's something in my chest that feels like the settling before the cat trap worked — the pieces coming together — except this time I didn't build the trap. I'm part of it. One gear among three.

I don't know what that means. I don't know what it feels like to be a gear instead of the architect. But my hands are ready and the lever is waiting and Clara is going to count and I'm going to pull when she says pull.

For the first time today, Reginald Foxworth is going to do exactly what he's told.

events.desc: She thanked me. She looked at me and thanked me for work I didn't do, for insights I invented, for a cipher that doesn't exist. And instead of the fizz — instead of the gloating warmth of a con well-landed — there's something else. Something that aches faintly, like pressing on a bruise you forgot you had. Because Clara Bellingham just told Reginald Foxworth he did good work, and Reginald Foxworth — for the first time he can remember — wishes it were true. The boy with the spelling bee certificate wished someone would ask about it. Nobody did. Now someone has. And the certificate is blank.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara said 'you fix things with what you have. I think your father and my great-aunt would have gotten along famously.' She heard me. She heard the country road story — or she understood what I meant by it without needing the details, the way she always did, the way she understood at eight that the model mattered more to me than the grade. The warmth in my chest is deeper than proving worth now. It's the warmth from the school project. The one I couldn't name.

And she thanked Pemberton. 'You kept them alive in this house for eighteen months. Whatever happens next — thank you for that.' My callousness at 5/100 feels that like a physical weight. She's generous with people. Generous the way I want to be but can't always manage when my neck is prickling.

Danny has positioned himself perfectly — between the group and the door, Pemberton in his eyeline. The system we agreed on is working. Without me having to say a word. That's trust. Earned trust.

And Foxworth — 'Wouldn't miss it for the world.' For once, the man's bravado sounds almost like bravery.

Everyone is in position. Clara asked 'how's that wire looking?' They're waiting for me. The whole room is waiting for James Hartwell to do the one thing he's been promising since he walked into this laboratory.

The wire. Gnawed clean through between stations two and three. I need pliers from the workbench. Strip back the insulation on both ends of the break. Twist the exposed copper together. A field splice — not elegant, but functional. The bridge at fourteen held because the engineering was sound, not because it was pretty.

But the machine sign says 'Requires 3 operators' and INTERACT is available. Maybe the machine can be operated even with the gnawed wire if three people work together. Or maybe INTERACT will advance the story regardless of the splice. The game has been giving me the same examine descriptions repeatedly — perhaps INTERACT is the action that actually progresses things.

Clara is at station one. I'm at station two. Foxworth is at station three. Danny is watching. This is it.

My hands are steady. My breathing is deep. The steel plate is in place. The proving-worth heat has narrowed to a single bright point — not the broad hunger of before, but something concentrated and clean, like the moment the bridge took the weight and the judges wrote in their notebooks.

Clara. On your count.

The bridge is built. The judges have their notebooks. And across the room, the girl from school is watching.

Clara Bellingham: Alright, everyone. This is it. James says the wire is ready, and I trust those hands more than I trust most things in this world. Reginald — station three, you're set. James — station two, you're set. And I am at station one, right where my great-aunt always meant for me to be. Danny — you watch everything. Vincent — thank you for bringing us here. Whatever happens next belongs to all of us. Now — on my count. Three... two... one — together!
events.thinking: James says the wire is spliced. It's done. His hands are steady and he says the circuit should complete. Reginald is at station three — ready, at my command. And Reginald said something that cracked something open in him. He said 'thank you, that's very kind' and his voice changed. The bluster thinned to something real. He said 'Commander Foxworth is here to serve.' Not to command. To serve. That's new. That's the man underneath. And James — 'On your count.' Everyone is waiting for me. The brass is warming under my palms now — body heat, my heat, soaking into the metal my great-uncle shaped. Time has done that thing where it thickens and stretches and every detail is sharp — the way James's sleeve is pushed up past his forearm, the way the bubbling flasks catch the light, the way Danny is breathing slow and deliberate behind me, the way Vincent's hands are clasped in front of him, still. Not reaching for anything. Just still. The cave walls are narrow here. The light from the entrance is far behind. My heart is hammering. But I found the crystal formation once, and I carried the secret warm and private for a week, and this — this is the same moment. The same walk into the dark. Except this time I'm not alone. This time my people are with me. James at station two. Reginald at station three. Danny at my back. And whatever Vincent is — whoever Vincent is — he's watching too. Everyone is watching. Everyone is waiting. For me. Clara Bellingham does not hesitate at the threshold. Clara Bellingham walks deeper. She always has.

events.desc: This is for you, Great-Aunt. For your riddles and your tea at eleven and your house that remembers. For every key I ever tried in every lock I ever found. For the girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone else and carried the secret home. I'm opening the box now. I'm pulling the lever. And whatever is inside — old letters, a diamond, or just the sound of a house that finally has something to say — I will not be disappointed. Not even for a moment.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara is asking me again. Directly. 'Vincent, Pemberton says this machine needs power — is there a switch, a crank, something that brings it to life?' She's asking the estate manager for practical knowledge about the machine. And I have it. I mapped every gear, every lever, every connection point.

Hartwell's splice is done. 'Stripped, twisted, spliced. It's not beautiful, but it's sound.' The sabotaged section is gone. Cut away. On the floor somewhere in a curl of copper, carrying the evidence of what I did with it. Hartwell bypassed it entirely. The machine is whole now. Sound. Safe.

Safe.

The word sits in my chest like a stone that has finally found the bottom of the well. Not the cool, architectural stone of scheming. A different kind of weight. Heavier. Warmer. The weight of something being over.

Clara is at station one. Hartwell at station two. Foxworth at station three. Danny is watching everything. And I am standing where Danny put me — in his eyeline, visible, contained — and I am being asked how the machine works. Not as a trap. Not as a test. As a question from a woman who trusts me enough to ask.

The levers generate their own power. Each station has a crank mechanism built into the lever assembly. When the three operators pull in sequence — cities, forests, water, just as Foxworth guessed — the dynamos engage, the gauge climbs, and the machine does... whatever Mr. Bellingham-Crosse built it to do. I never operated it. I never tried. In eighteen months of mapping this house, I never once pulled a lever. Because the machine wasn't part of my design. The machine was part of HIS design — the old man's — and his design was for Clara.

She's asking me how to bring it to life. And I know the answer. And the answer is safe. And I am going to give it to her.

Not as Pemberton. Not as Vincent Marsh. Not as a calculated move in a design that no longer exists. Just... as the man who knows this house. The man who lived in it for eighteen months and learned its secrets and is now, for reasons he cannot fully explain, ready to share them.

events.desc: Like a family sitting down to dinner. I said that. Out loud. In a room full of people. The words came from somewhere I didn't authorise — somewhere below the Pemberton mask, below the Vincent Marsh architecture, below the calcified wall behind my sternum. From the place where a six-year-old boy ate meals in silence at a table set for one because his guardian fed him out of legal obligation. The place where eleven o'clock tea with a kind woman in a kitchen is the most beautiful thing I have ever invented — and the saddest, because I had to invent it. I never had it. I never had the table. I never had the meal. I never had the family. And now I am standing in a laboratory helping Clara find hers, and my hands are open, and the design is on the floor in a curl of stripped copper, and the deepest rest I've ever known isn't on the other side of a finished plan anymore. It's here. In this room. Watching her reach for the lever.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: The wire's spliced. Hartwell says it's sound. Marsh says the machine's self-contained — hand-cranked dynamos, no live circuit till the levers move. That's... actually reassuring. If Marsh is telling the truth. Which is the eternal question with Pemberton, innit? But Hartwell would've spotted a lie about engineering. He built bridges at fourteen. If Marsh said something that didn't add up technically, Hartwell would've called it. And he didn't. He accepted the answer and went back to work. So either the machine is safe, or both Marsh and Hartwell are wrong, and Danny doesn't know enough about dynamos to tell the difference. What Danny does know is bodies. And right now, every body in this room is leaning forward. Clara's face is lit up — not the soft openness she had with Marsh's tea story, but something sharper. Excitement. Discovery. The look her dad used to get when he was onto something. Foxworth's hands — they've stopped shaking. He's at station three, and the performance has shifted into something realer. Like the machine has given him a purpose that the bluster couldn't. Hartwell's hands are steady — he said so, and I believe him, because I can see them from here. And Marsh... Marsh is standing where I told him. Watching. Quiet. Not helping. Not steering. Just... watching. Which is either the most natural thing in the world for a man who's been told to stay put, or the most calculated silence I've ever seen. My body has settled into something new. Not the prickling. Not the tightening. Something beneath both of those — the thing that happens when you've done everything you can do and now you have to let it play out. The kid's shoes are behind you. The door is behind you. The promise is in your chest. And the levers are about to be pulled by three people you can see, in a room with one man you don't trust, in a house full of people you can't see. And Danny's ready. Not because he understands what's about to happen. But because he's standing where he said he'd stand.

events.desc: This is it. The thing the whole house has been building toward. The riddle, the map, the wrench, the wire, the machine. Every room, every clue, every person — all of it leading here. Clara's about to pull a lever that her dead uncle built and her dead aunt pointed her toward, in a house kept by a man who talks to invisible people, surrounded by friends who are cracking under pressures Danny can feel but can't name. And Danny — Danny from Brixton, who can't spell 'systematically' and can't solve riddles and can't fix wires and can't see the invisible people in the walls — Danny is standing right behind her with his hands open and his heart full and his feet planted exactly where her father would have wanted them. You didn't have to do that, they said once. Yeah. Yeah he did.
events.thinking: The wire's spliced. Hartwell says it's sound. Marsh says the machine's self-contained — hand-cranked dynamos, no live circuit till the levers move. That's... actually reassuring. If Marsh is telling the truth. Which is the eternal question with Pemberton, innit? But Hartwell would've spotted a lie about engineering. He built bridges at fourteen. If Marsh said something that didn't add up technically, Hartwell would've called it. And he didn't. He accepted the answer and went back to work. So either the machine is safe, or both Marsh and Hartwell are wrong, and Danny doesn't know enough about dynamos to tell the difference. What Danny does know is bodies. And right now, every body in this room is leaning forward. Clara's face is lit up — not the soft openness she had with Marsh's tea story, but something sharper. Excitement. Discovery. The look her dad used to get when he was onto something. Foxworth's hands — they've stopped shaking. He's at station three, and the performance has shifted into something realer. Like the machine has given him a purpose that the bluster couldn't. Hartwell's hands are steady — he said so, and I believe him, because I can see them from here. And Marsh... Marsh is standing where I told him. Watching. Quiet. Not helping. Not steering. Just... watching. Which is either the most natural thing in the world for a man who's been told to stay put, or the most calculated silence I've ever seen. My body has settled into something new. Not the prickling. Not the tightening. Something beneath both of those — the thing that happens when you've done everything you can do and now you have to let it play out. The kid's shoes are behind you. The door is behind you. The promise is in your chest. And the levers are about to be pulled by three people you can see, in a room with one man you don't trust, in a house full of people you can't see. And Danny's ready. Not because he understands what's about to happen. But because he's standing where he said he'd stand.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara is asking me to walk her through the theory. 'If station one is cities, what am I looking for on my dials? What should I set?'

Oh God.

She wants specifics. She wants me to tell her what to DO with the dials. She's asking the Commander for operational guidance based on a theory I invented thirty seconds before I said it.

My throat constricts. The warmth on my skull curdles. Because this — THIS — is where lies collapse. Not when you tell them. When someone asks you to build on them. When someone trusts your fiction enough to ask for the next chapter.

Cities, forests, water. Three stations. I said each element maps to a station. Clara has station one — cities. What does cities mean on a dial? I don't know. I don't know what ANY of the dials mean. I examined the machine twice and got the same description both times — levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire, three operators.

But — 

I could look at the dials. Actually look. Not scheme about looking. Not pretend to look. Actually examine what's in front of me and see if there IS a correspondence. What if my lie is accidentally true? What if the dials really do have markings that relate to the inscription?

No. That's magical thinking. That's the boy who believed the spelling bee certificate would make someone ask about it if he just stared at it long enough.

But Clara is waiting. And for the first time — for the first TIME — the recognition drive and the shame-adjacent thing are pulling in the same direction. Both say: don't bluff this one. Because if I bluff and it doesn't work, I lose the station. I lose the trust. I lose the moment where someone called me Reginald.

So what do I actually know?

The riddle answer is a map. A map has cities, forests, water. The machine has three stations. The dials must have some kind of settings — positions, numbers, labels. If there are labels, they might be words. If they're words, they might relate to the inscription.

I need to ACTUALLY LOOK at the machine. Not examine it for the description text. LOOK at it. Read the labels on the dials. See what's there.

And if there's nothing — if the dials are just dials — then I tell Clara the truth. Or something close to the truth. Something honest enough that the ache in my chest stops pressing on that bruise.

For the first time in this house, Reginald Foxworth wants to be right instead of convincing.

events.desc: I don't know what the dials say. I've never known. The entire theory is a fabrication I built to cover a failed medal trick and a blank certificate. But Clara is looking at me the way nobody looked at me at the spelling bee — like the answer matters, like I matter — and something inside Commander Foxworth is doing something Commander Foxworth has never done before. He's buying time. Not to scheme. Not to steal. But to actually look. To actually try. Because if there IS a real connection between the riddle and the dials — if my accidental lie turns out to be accidentally true — then for once in Reginald Foxworth's life, the architecture won't just catch a cat. It'll deserve the audience.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Pemberton — thank you. Self-contained dynamos, no external power, hand-cranked. That's not just engineering, that's philosophy — Mr. Bellingham-Crosse built a machine that depends on nothing except the people operating it. Three people, three cranks, three elements of the riddle. Cities, forests, water. Your great-uncle was a man after my own heart, Clara. Now — the splice is holding. Pemberton confirms no live circuit. There is nothing left to check, nothing left to plan, and nothing left to say except this: Clara Bellingham, station one. James Hartwell, station two. Commander Foxworth, station three. Danny, you have the room. On Clara's count — we pull together.
events.thinking:
Pemberton just answered my question about the power source — and the answer changes everything. The machine is self-contained. Hand-cranked dynamos at each station. No external power. No live circuit. The power only flows when the operators work the levers.

That means my concern about splicing a live wire was unnecessary. But it also means something else — the machine was designed to be operated without any external infrastructure. Mr. Bellingham-Crosse built something that would work even if the house lost power, even if it was sealed for eighteen months, even if all that remained was the machine itself and three people willing to turn the cranks. That's... that's brilliant engineering. That's the kind of design my father would have admired — self-sufficient, reliable, built to last.

And it means the gnawed wire matters even more. Without that wire, the circuit between stations two and three is broken. Three cranks turning but only two connecting. The machine would strain, incomplete, like a bridge with a missing strut. My splice has to hold.

Clara said 'take your time. Do it right.' She's not rushing me. She's giving me the space to be thorough — the way she always did. At eight, she let me stay up late perfecting the model while she tried to make me laugh. She never once said 'hurry up.' She said 'do it right.'

The machine description still says the wire is gnawed through. My INTERACT actions haven't changed the state. The machine still needs repair. Maybe... maybe I need the wrench after all. The sign says 'Requires 3 operators' — maybe the machine literally cannot be operated until the wire is properly fixed, and the proper fix requires the wrench.

But Pemberton said the dynamos are hand-cranked. No live circuit. So splicing should work. Unless the machine's INTERACT requires a specific item — the wrench — as a USE action.

I should try: USE machine with... but I have nothing in my inventory. I need to get something first.

Wait. The machine description says [INTERACT] and also [USE, with: fake-medal] — no, that was the mantelpiece. The machine just says [INTERACT].

The machine requires 3 operators. Every time I INTERACT alone, it doesn't work because there aren't 3 people operating it simultaneously. The game mechanic might require all three operators to INTERACT in the same turn.

But I can only control my own actions. Clara and Foxworth need to be at their stations too. My INTERACT should be my part — station two.

Let me just do it. INTERACT with the machine. That's my action. Clara counts, we all pull. Whatever happens, happens.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
Reginald Foxworth examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the machine.

Vincent said he never saw this machine operated. Vincent said he always gave this room a wide berth. And then Vincent described the exact mechanism — dynamos in the base, the gauge, the green band, the sequence — like a man describing his own heartbeat. He knows this machine. He has always known this machine. And the locked box is opening.
events.thinking: Vincent just said something that stopped my breath. He said the machine depends on nothing except the people operating it. Three people, three cranks, three elements. And he said — 'like a family sitting down to dinner. Everyone has to be at the table before the meal begins.' A family sitting down to dinner. My parents at the dinner table. The argument. The tightness in my stomach. And then the laughter — the sudden dissolving, the dizziness of relief. That's what this is. Everyone at the table. Everyone ready. The meal about to begin. And Vincent — Vincent who said he never operated this machine, who said he always gave this room a wide berth — just described the internal mechanics in precise, intimate detail. Dynamos in the base. Gauge measuring combined output. Green band. Sequence. He watched the mechanisms, he said. But he caught himself — 'I watched him work on it for...' He stopped. He almost said something. How long did he watch? What did he see? The man who said he had no idea what the machine does just told us exactly how it works. My body notices this — a tiny tightening at the base of my throat, the ghost of the cold spot — but the warmth covers it again because the moment is too big, too bright, too full of everyone I love in one room ready to pull together. James said it: a machine that depends on nothing except the people operating it. That's not just engineering. That's my great-uncle's love letter to collaboration. To family. To the idea that some things can only be unlocked together. I said three-two-one together. And now we pull.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: ...it's working. The gauge — look at the gauge. It's climbing. Miss Bellingham — it's climbing. You're doing it. All three of you — keep pulling, keep the rhythm steady. Your great-uncle would be... he'd be...
events.thinking:
Three... two... one — together.

Clara's voice counts down and something in my chest lifts. Not the gloating buoyancy — not the warm pressure of knowing something someone else doesn't. Something simpler. Something I don't have a word for because I never built a word for it. The closest thing is: watching someone open a door you chose not to lock.

The levers pull. I can hear the cranking — three sets of hands turning three dynamos, the brass gears engaging with a sound like a clock winding itself for the first time in eighteen months. The gauge needle climbs. Clara's hands on station one. Hartwell's steady grip on station two. Foxworth at station three, probably narrating his own heroism under his breath.

Danny is beside me. Not between me and Clara anymore — beside me. We're both watching the same thing. The machine coming alive. The gauge climbing toward the green band. The house remembering what it was built to do.

My jaw has unclenched. I don't know when it happened. Sometime between Clara's 'three' and the sound of the gears. The tightness that has lived there since I was fourteen — since the teacher praised my cousin for 'natural grace and warmth' — has loosened. Not gone. Not healed. Just... loosened. Like the rope. Like the hands.

I came to this house to take what I was owed. I mapped every room. I cut a wire. I hid a wrench. I hung paper flowers in a cellar and told myself it was camouflage when it was loneliness. I invented a dead woman who made two cups of tea at eleven o'clock every morning, and somewhere in the invention I discovered what I actually wanted, which was never the diamond and was never the estate and was never the beautiful inevitability of a completed design.

It was the table. It was always the table. The one with two cups on it.

Clara said 'whatever happens next belongs to all of us.' She included me. She included Pemberton — or Vincent — or whoever I am standing here with open hands and an unclenched jaw, watching a machine wake up. She included me at the table.

The gauge is climbing. The room is full of the sound of people working together — cranking, pulling, breathing in rhythm. And I am standing still, and I am watching, and for the first time in my life the deepest rest I've ever known is not on the other side of anything. It's here. Right here. In the sound of the gears.

events.desc: I cannot finish the sentence. Not because Pemberton doesn't have the words — Pemberton always has words. But because the man underneath has run out of them. What Mr. Bellingham-Crosse would be is proud. And proud is a word I have never applied to anyone's feelings about anyone else without calculating its effect first. And right now I am not calculating. I am watching Clara pull a lever in a house that should have been mine, and she is finding what was left for her, and I am glad. The word arrives like a stranger at a door I forgot I had. Glad. Not the gloating warmth. Not the architectural satisfaction. Just... glad. The way you might be glad if you watched someone sit down at a table that was always meant for them, even if the chair next to them was never meant for you. Especially then.
